blv DrAn NELLIE, The shape in hats (as distinguished from toques), , that is favoured above the rest, has a very low crown and a wide brim that droops in front and at the back, but is slightly raised at the sides. .'lometimes this Lrirß is double, and the upper one is bent sharply up here and there, the straw being always of the lightest and most flexible kind. A model which is pretty, carried out in almost any colour, is of satin-straw; the brim is veiled with cream lace, a large bow of chine ribbon with a buckle in the centre is placed in front of the crown and clusters of flowers are tucked under the brim at the sides. Next to these flat, drooping hats in order of popularity come the many shapes in Tuscan, Leghorn, and fancy straws, that have high, narrow crowns and brims crumpled-up in so-called rustic fashion: A very becoming specimen of this style, of deep cream-colour Italian straw, has the crown encircled by a twist of black glace silk; the brim is sharply bent up above the forehead with a big chtiu of black silk. A pretty hat of Leghorn is trimmed entirely with white soft satin ribbon, and is really an ideal hat for a girl to wear at a garden-party or country Me, and another pretty model is of cream straw with lines of green running through it, and is trimmed with deeper green velvet and an eagle quilL- The main part of the trimming of this hat is planed a little to the left of the front, at which point the brim is slightly raised; at the back it is bent into flutes, as it were, and aurves closely down on the hair. Rush hats in greenish-grey, and cream shades, trimmed with chinCribbon or soft silk scarves, are nice for everyday wear; while for cycling and travelling the boat-shape in pliable straw, ornamented with a band and bow of water- proof ribbon and a quill, is more in vogue than the sailor hat.

When the home aressmaker essay§ the task co making a blouse or bodice for herself, or indeed anyone else, it is necessary to be provided with a really good pattern. For this purpose the lining of an old bodice whose fit has been altogether satisfactory in the past will often prove the very thing, after it has been subjected to careful un- picking from the material itself, followed by a thorough brushing to remove all possible dust, which might soil any delicate material. The lining should then be damped and carefully pressed with a hot iron, particular pains being taken to smooth out the seams, while any notches must be pressed into shape, as they may be of untold significance in obtaining a good fit when one part is fitted to another. A pattern of thiii description, if originally designed by the hand of a thoroughly well-trained and skilful dressmaker, is altogether desirable, but it is not everyone whose means even in the near past has permitted her in- dulgence in a gown created by a first-class modiste. It is, therefore, left to her to fall back on a good paper pattern. These can be zot, as you know, in several sizes' but it is a wiser plan to go to the expense of a little extra outlay and have such cut to measure.

The cut of skirts in thinner materials will ot necessity vary somewhat from those of more sub- stantial stuff. lheFie gain their fulness round the feet usually by means of an added flounce, a volant en forme. flu". in thin fabrica this flounce would drop out of shape, and sag is an ugly fashion; therefore cotton skirts though equally full, will have darts round the hips, and then the seams from the knees will be cut sharply slanting and gores inserted, so that when two are joined together, it will give the appearance of a full flounce. Bat too well-fitting a skirt in cotton materials is seldom pretty. They look much better if gathered and fulled into the waistband in what is known as the housemaid-skirt style. The under-petticoat, which is separate from the skirt proper, should be much frilled round the bottom to keep the fulness out well from the feet.

Flowers sn(l ribbons are the prevailing trim. on evening gowns. Bowers fall in long trails from the back of the left shoulder on to the skirt of the dress, or are caught across the front of the bodice from left to right, fastened in at the waist. Others, mixed with ropes of chiffon, form wide sashes at tho side of the skirt, usually attached to the dress here and there. On lace dresses sometimes a trail of flowers is laid right across the front of the skirt, stitched down in a few places. So beautiful are the artificial blossoms that their employment in every department of dress possible is to be heartily welcomed. Every hat, if it follow the mode, may be dubbed a flower hat, for one and all are laden and often covered with dowers of some kind. Your loving JENNIL
FRIDAY, MAY 3, 1901

div.head: FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES.
THE JOINT UNIONS.

The joint meetings of the Baptist and Con- gregational Unions in London on April :23 and 25 mark an epoch in the history of the ancient Dissenters of England. Not for many years, if ever, have thesti two Unions had simultaneously as their official heads men of such distinction as Dr. Joseph Parker and Dr. Alex. Maclaren Unfortunately, there were many complaints as to the distribution of tickets and the choice of the meeting place. • The City Temple can accommodate at a push 3000 people, whereas the number of persons who were entitled to be present is somewhere about double that number. It was asked " Why wee not the Albert Ball taken r The one conclusive answer to that was that not even Dr. Parker could make himself heard in eery corner of that spacious building, and Dr. Machiren, we believe, absolutely. refused to attempt ,to address an audience there: The joint meetings of the unions may lead to a closer intercourse between the Baptist and Congregational Churches throughout the country. Some persons, indeed, - are bold enough to anticipate that the gatherings are the prelude to a great corporate union of the two denominations. But the need of that and the desire fur it are not as yet obvious.

div.head: OPEN-AIR PREACHING.
div.p: OPEN-AIR PREACHING.

The Free Churches are exercising themselves sta to how best to follow up the Simultaneous Mission. The Rev. Thomas Law, the Organising Secretary pf the National Council, has, at the request of the General Committee, issued a circular to all the Councils urging them to make arrangements for open - air services during the coming summer. Mr. Law suggests half-past eight in the evening as a suitable time for ministers and Christian workers. These open-air services will be conducted by the best men that. the Free Churches have, and , with the aid of united choirs will be made as ' attractive as possible. It is recognised that open-air work has fallen somewhat into disre- pute, by being too much in the hands of men whose zeal exceeds their tact and knowledge. The outside masses are not to be attracted by bad preaching. It is believed that during the coming summer England will witness an open- air evangelistic campaign as great and as fruit- ful as the Simultaneous Mission early in the year.

THE FREE CHURCH YEAR EOM We have received an ad' ance copy of the Free Church Year Book, issued by the Publica- tion Department of the National Free Church Council. It contains full reports of the recent Cardiff meetings, and a great mass Of valuable Free Church information. Most readers will probably turn at once to the part in which Mr. Howard Evans deal with Free Church statistics. -Mr. Evans, whose accuracy has never been seriousl7 disputed, says that the membership 14 i of the Free Churches s now 1,910,302 and of the Established Church 1,941,760. Although the membership of the Established Church is somewhat larger than that of the Free Churches, the Free Churches provide accommodation for many more persons. Their sittings number 8,100,652, and the sittings of the Anglican Church 6,979,150. The Free Churches have 384,632 Sunday-school teachers, the Estab- lished Church has 207,539. The Free Churches have 3,283,608 Sunday-school scholars, and the Established Church has 2,866,291. The total membership of the Free Churches all over the world is above seventeen millions, and of the Anglican Church over three millions. The im- portance and significance of these figures will not be disputed. The Year Book, which is tastefully got up, is pablietied at fs.6d net. TAN CRAIRMALIN OF THE LONDON COUNTY
t7OUNCIL.

The May Fr eP Church Chronicle has an interest- ing sketch of Mr. A. M. Torrance,the new Chair- man of the London County Council. Mr. Torrance, who is an Ayrshire man, is a member of Highbury-quadrant Congregational Church, of which the Rev. W. J. Dawson, of literary repute, is pastor. Mr. Torrance is superinten- dent of the Sunday-school, and for many years has taken an active part in Church work. He is a quiet, genial and forceful man. The article is illustrated with a fine photograph of Mr. Torrance. The same number contains a sketch with portrait of Mr. W. R. Lane, one of the National Council's missioners. Mr. Lane was for over four years in the Cold- stream Guards and has had an eventful career. The late Mr. D. L. Moody had a keen regard for him, and at his invitation Mr. Lane delivered a series of lectures at the Chicago Bible In- stitute. Mr. Lane also enjoyed the friendship of the Rev. C. H. Spurgeon. The article con- tains some interesting anecdotes. CON GREGATIONLL MISSIONS IN LONDON. The Wesleyan Methodists were the first to discover that the way to reach the masses in the centres of our great cities was to convert old decayed chapels into mission centres. The success of the Manchester Wesleyan Mission and other enterprises of the same sort in our great towns has abundantly justified the wisdom and sagacity of the leaders of the for- ward movement. The London Congregational Union, noting the signs of the times, has re- solved to establish four mission centres in the metropolis. The first one will be at Pentonville, where a languishing cause, Claremont Chapel, is to be re-opened next summer as the head of the North London Congregational Mission. Several thousand pounds will be required for initial expenses, and an annual income of at least !.:4000 will be required for the maintenance of these four great centres. Mr. %V. H. Brown, the present Chairman of the London Union, is taking great interest in the scheme. For thirty years Mr. Brown has by personal service and financial help supported evangelistic efforts in some of the poorest parts of London. We trust this new spirited enterprise will be crowned with abundant success. THE REV. HUGH PRICE HUGHES, M.A. We are glad to hear that Mr. Price Hughes is making a good recovery from his illness, and that he hopes shortly to be in the midst of his -work again. Probably Mr. Hughes will take more care in the future not to over- burden himself. We observe that he has resigned the presidency of the Million Tempe- rance Pledges Crusade, to which he was elected enly a few months ago. Paragraphs have appeared in the Press as to Mr. Hughes's in- tention to visit Australia. We believe that this visit has already been fixed, but that it will not take place until the autumn of next year.
THE PASTORS' COLLEGE.

The Pastors' College at the Metropolitan Tabernacle, founded by the Rev. C. H. Spurgeon, continues to flourish. Not a tithe of the students who seek admission can be received. One of the students, Mr. Whitehouse, who had only just left Eng- land with his w he, has been murdered in China. He is the first man from the college to seal his faith with his blood. Altogether 1019 students have passed through the college. Six hundred an:l fifty-four are still labouring as pastors, I:6Bs:toners' and evangelists. The income for the 3:oar has more than met the expenses. This is undoubtedly a splendid record. The late C. IL Spurgeon's skill as au organiser is shown in nothing more clearly than in this—that his institutions have aill anntinued to flourish with undiminished swami am his death.

The Royal National Lifeboat Institution is one of many Societies that has suffered a falling off of contri- butions owing to the war. For this reason several leading women in society have decided to give an enter- tainment in aid of the "Lifeboat Saturday Fund,"which will take place at Stafford House on June 26th. There will be a grand concert and an illumination of the gardens, and the Duchess of Sutherland,nsver wearying of any good cause, will act as hostess. Among others who are kindly assisting in the arrangements for the lens, are the Dowager Duchess of Argyll, the Duchess of Devonshire, Katherine, Ductless of Westminster, the Marchioness of Londonderry, the Duchess of Montrose, and Lady Tweedniouth. This will be one of the prircipat events of the London season,and as the accommodation will be limited it is expected that the tickets will realise quite fancy prices. The postponed celebrations of the coming of age of the Duke of Westminster. and his marriage with MiSS Cornwallis-West, are to take place this month, and Eton Hall will be en fete for three days, from the 21st to the 24th. First the coming of age festivities had to be put off last year, owing to the absence of the Duke in South Africa, and the wedding was a quiet affair owing to the death of our late Queen. The two events will now be celebrated by extensive rejoicings, including a garden party, and entertainment at the Hall, dinners for the tenantry and cottagers,and various treats and festivities for over 6.000 school children. The Duke it seem, dees not intend to sever his connection with the Army, aid has recently taken a house at Windsor, where he will stay when on duty with the Royal Horse Guards. The engagement is announced of Miss Edith Wills to Mr Percy Douglas Hamilton, heir presumptive of the Duke of Hamilton. The bride elect is the eldest daugh- ter of Sir Frederick Willa who is a member of the large. and wealthy family of Bristol, and whose firm is so well- known to all lovers of tobacco. Miss Wills is a very attractive and accomplished girl, and her mother Lady I Wills is the daughter of a Lanarkshire minister. She is I therefore not wholly unconnected with Scotland the , borne of tho magnificent Hamilton Palace, over which she may some day be called upon to preside. It was said in the House of Commons the other day that a majnrity of women are not in favour of permitting a man to marry the sister of a deceased wife. If that were the case, it would constitute the strongest areu- client against the Bill, that has so long been the sutjset of a strenuous agitation to pass into law. The experi- ence of other countries however doss not support the view that women as a rule are oppose d to this reform,— insch is certainly not the case in our own Colonies, and this country would hardly steed alone, amongst the nations of the world, in refusing to legalise such Inarriazop. if the great bulk of feminine opinion was spier these. It is quite certain that the long struggle over the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill, will end in its passing into law, and that before very long. The recent discussion shows that the new House of Commons is overwhelm- ingly in favour of the measure, and it is evident that , much of the old ecclesiastical prejudice against the Bill ,is gradually dying out. If the two Houses of Parliament eould be induced to deal with the subject in a straight- forward end business like way, there is no doubt that the present Bill would pass into law. But once mere the intricacies of Parliamentary procedure seems like!, to wreck it, and, in spite of the great majority of 157 recorded in its favour in the House of Commons, it doss nst seem likely to attain its final success this session. The King. as is arch-known is in favour oe this is form, and it is thought that his accession will have some in- fluence in bringing the two Houses of Parliament more into line upon this subject, but the two branches of our Legislature are so much given to evasion and to tin ways of contrary,that the difficulty is to get them to act togetber,and deal finally with the Bill. The wide brims of many of the hats destined for early summer wear, are showing hand painted trails of flowers and foliage. Needless to say, such headgear is by no means inexpensive. But in the end, matters are about even, for such hate require very little in the way of trimming—indeed much ornamentation wouli, from an artistic point of view, be fatal. Swathed in chiffon, and raised on the left side by a cluster of flowers and foiege to match those portrayed on the brim, this particular style of headgear is calculated to satisfy the most fastidious and exclusive among us. Narrow black velvet ribbon, run through lace, and open-work fabrics, bag become too popular to suit fashionable modistes, who are now utilising in is steed, narrow silver braid, or white t ete velvet ribbon. Tire former run through lace makes delightfully cool, smelt- looking yeets,or chemisettes,and the latterehough by no means so scent mini as the bile* variety, gives • much more /hie and soft effect to the materials which it adorns. Yet another innovation in the world of trim- mings, is a garniture of twine—common kitchen twine —studded with gems ! This combination of simplicity and extravagance is almost ludicrous, snd is not likely to be indulged in, save by the very few. For some time past there have been signs that for evening, elaborate bead-dressing will be the rule, this coming season, instead of the exception. A tiny wreath La go round the knot of hair, comprised of small flowers and leaves (to match or blend with the toilette) a whime or black marabout plume rising from it, is now donned by many up-to-date woman, and usquestionably this gives a deligh' ful finish to a well-dressed head. Hair. ornaments of divers descriptions have fieurei largely among the wedding presents of fashionable brides lately and very beautiful and costly the majority of these have been. The many fatal accidents arising out of the use of curling tongs frequently find confirmation in the annals of the Coroner's Courts. Nor do these always arise from the dangerous spirit lamp, as a case was retorded in London the other day where a girl made her tongs red hot in the fire and ret her clothing alight with them, with fatal results. On board many ocean liner., the use of spirit lamps by the passengers is absolutely for- bidden, and on some of the newest ships'on the Atlantic service, connections for electric hair marling irons dr,' provided in the ladies' cabins. This saves all trouble, and at the same time ensures safety. Speaking of electric-bested curling tongs, One wonders when we shall have these, and other luxuires in our homes, such as we have long been promised in this new age of e!setricity. W e are, for instance, promised east at twopence per thousand feet, and electricity at loss than a twentieth of its present cost, and this too, by Dr Ludwig Mond, who is no mere visionary, but one of the greatest and best- known scientists of the present day. It is therefore not too much to hope that some day we may be ab e to (1,, all our lighting, cooking, and housewarming by electric- ity. That, when it comes!, will lighten the work in our homes to an extent which can hardly he retimated in words. To those who struggle with their own house- work it will prove an immense boon, while to those who now depend upon the assistance of one or tor, domestics, it will be a great retie'', since it will render :bona v ry much more independent of (grvants.

div.head: ECCENTRICITIES OF "WADERS."
div.p: THE ECCENTRICITIES OF "WADERS."

" The grcup of British birds whose habits and eccen- tricities are probably least known to the unscientifi- reader is that of the • Waders.' They haunt the desoc late and waste places of the earth, and but tor their pre- sence our lens, marshes, meres, uplands, and shores would be almost unbroken eelitudes and silence. Although their lives are spent in such lonely places, they seem to make up for this isolation by being in them- selves pecuiia rty sprightly, sociable, and conversational; they are, in fact, decidedly "(luscious. 'Waders' are chiefly to be met with it. the tidal hex hours, creeks, or rn the mud-flats of the c aat. In such places, at low water, little parties or flocks may be seen running hither and thither over the sands, or wading through the aballow pools in search of food Is ft by the receding tide. Some species delight in feeding even in the very surf of the sea, rush- ing to secure some delicimus morsel from a retreating wave, lightly skipping aside as it advances again. At high tide, however, when the sea has covered the flats and drivs n the birds reluctantly from their feedlot.- grounds, they repair to the shingly beach or to f OMB neighbouring field, there to idle away the time, All the activity and energy displayed in the pursuit of food is eonet The birds stand or tit lounging about in little I groups, perhaps passing a few casual remarks. the greatest exertion now indulged in being the occasional preening and re-arranging of some refractory feather, or a desultory stretch of wing or limb. Whilst reeting thee, especially on wet, marshy ground, they seem to prefer standing on one leg. The leg drawn up, having been previously shaken violently, to dry it, is introduced into the feathers of the breast on trial ; hut ehould the bird no, be Satisfied, the drying process is repeated. (Nice the limb is thoroughly warm under the plumage it, owner is very loth to rep`ace it on the mud, so much so that even when busted be its companions or some larger spec'es it will hop out of the way on one foot. In tie same manner it will search for and pick up food, often proceeding considerable distances, and se f mingly pr. - ferrine t his tsrdy means of locomotion to exi,ceure ot , the limb. Only when an exceptionally strong gust ot I wind, sweeping over the maisn, threatens to carry it sterav bodily, does it hastily restore itself to a biped ,I I - condition. Often, too, while thus resting on one leg, with the till and head tucked away snugly amongtt tie feathers rf the back, the same sort of cone:wet is dis— played. Wishing to see objects not in view from its snug position, yet unwilling to expose the head, it will, swing the body round as on a pivot, until the necessary survey is completed. It is most amusing to watch the swaying movements of a score of little feather balls and the inquisitive backward glances of twice as many beady black eyes as some fresh arrival appears in their midst. Although to all appearances an unwary little band, vet they will be found exceedingly difficult of a roach. The reason is not far to eeek. In every flock there !seem to he two or three members who neither slumber nor sleep.A niping alarm note from one of these sentinels is eneugh to arsruse the little day-dreamers and thB biros quickly take flight to some secluded spot. This system 01 mounting guard is particularly noticeable in the various species of Plovers. A sentit el Golden Plover cuts quite a eoldierelikes figure as he stands to attention co some eminence, his form sharply silhouetted against the sky, cr acing hie neck and standing on the very tips nf his toes, thlebetter to view some suspicious opject.' —From the May number of the " Wiudsor Magazine.'

div.head: Copyrig
div.p: Copyrig
THE LADDER OF GUILT.
BY TILYSS ROGERS, Anti)°Or of "For L 0943 and the Queen," "'Wedded
in Mystery," Spa,

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: Douglas Low, madly in love with Grace Hendon, daughter of a neighbouring farmer, attempts to murder his zousin Martin Fenwick. His aim, however, un- accountablyfails, and Squire Feuwick, his uncle, is the victim instead. The deed was witnessed by an old hag who has a grudge against the Fenwicks, and who accuses Martin of the murder. MArtin is tried and found guilty. The execution fails, and a second attempt a week later is also abortive. Martin. Fenwick is reprieved, and removed to a convict prison.

div.head: CHAPTER VIII.
div.p: CHAPTER VIII.
THE FIRE AT THE BARTON.

It was freezing in the open, though it was only the late autumn still by the calendar. Winter seemed to have stolen an advance march on the seasons and had appeared before his time. The heavy dew of the early evening was eapidly turning to cold, dank hoar-frost, and by ten o'clock the moon' looked down bright and chilly upon a beautiful, but , frost-bound countryside. The trees in the drive leading up to Fenwick Chas* stood like ghostly sentinelk; shivering and sighing as the breeze played among their cold and recently- stripped branches. . _

s light shone boldly forth from one of the windows of the house, shedding a lurid glow over the dew-drop ,frosted lawn. Inside, buried in the capacious depths of a huge - armchair, sat Douglas Low. He had dined remarkably well, and the whisky on the occasional table at his side was of the choicest quality. As a matter of fact, Ms, Douglas Low was just at that Feint when the British publican, with an eye to the proper reten- tion of his licence, would have mentally marked him for only one glass more. But there was no British publican to draw the limit line of sobriety in Fenwick Chase, and as Jarvis, Low's man, would have been prepared to assert, it took his master an unconscionably long while to get into a condition needing his assistance. "Another will do no harm," said Low to him- self. Yet he laughed cynically as he muttered it, for he was clever enough to know himself, and could sneer at his own follies without evincing a single desire to amend them. "Another and then to bed. Hum-drum, hum-drum. I'm sick to death of this. Yet I suppose I must be content, to bear it until Grace has been tamed. There was a little less of the almighty bounce about her, I fancied, in our interview of to-day. A life sentence takes a lot of time to work out, and she's tiring of her heroics about the matter already. Another six months of my management of this estate and— Hulloa What's that ?" • He had turned during his muttering to pour out the extra glass of whisky, but he was suddenly pulled up short with the glass in his hand by an apparition at the window. It wai-a man's face, an evil face, scored with deep lines, with a low fore- head and a hanging, thick-set chin, covered by a scrubby beard of three days' growth. A smile of familiarity overspread the hideous features. second later and the man outside had passed. Low waited a minute, sitting in a dazed stupor. Then he attempted to rise. "I wonder if the fool means to come in. I've warned him times enough, Heaven knows. rshall have to go a step further before i'm quite safe, I see." .

His soliloquy was cut short by a violent, ringing of the hall bell. LoW fell back into- his chair again. "Of course, of course," he said. "I might have known. More money, more money, I suppose. Curse him l " The door opened. Jarvis thrust in his head. ' "Mr. Parr to see you, sir," he said. "I told him it was too late, you couldn't see visitors at this hour, but he would not go away." "And quite right, too. Who gave you instruc- tions to turn my tenants away? It must be some- thing pressing for him to come to the Chase at this hour. Shaw him in.

Mr. Parr was accordingly ushered in. He was short, broad, and of coarse build, with the stamp of the gaol-bird marked on every line of his physiognomy, and he entered with the limp be had inherited from his birth.

"Yer don't seem pleased to see me," he said, as soon as Jervis was out of sight. "Wot, a little bit of a booze on all to yerself ? An' won't invite a friend to have a drop?" "Oh, of course, Parr. Help yourself, help _ _ _

yourself," said Low. "Pardon me, but I ought to have shewn more courtesy to a friend," he added. "Now, Mr. Low, don't be sarcastic. It don't some'ow fit the case. An' you never 'ad better friends on this earth than me and me mother, s'there now. I don't want to keep on a- mentionin' of it, on'y don't be too uppish on them as 'as done yer a good turn. Yer might 'aye come to the door yerself an' let me in an saved all this hettiketty an' foolin'. I give yer a look in as I was passin' on purpose." "Well, you're here, man, and isn't that enough? What's your business '

"The u-su-al," said Mr. Parr, with placid unction, spreading out his hands. "It's aggericul- tural depression, that's wet it is, I says. Any- how, we're fifty pounds behind in squarre up our accounts for the quarter, that's just it, an' we thought perhaps you'd like to 'elp your friends a bit.'

• "Haven't I paid you every halfpenny that's due to you for the next six months? Do you think I'm made of money that you can blood-suck me like this? I won't advance you another farthing. There, you can take that as your answer and con- found you!" It would not be too much to imagine that, after this somewhat forceful refusal to stand creditor, Mr. Low's visitor had beaten a rapid retreat. But this was precisely the opposite to the proceedings of Mr. Zeke Parr. Instead, he threw himself into n lounge opposite Low, poured himself out his second tumbler of whisky, seized a choice cigar from a box perched on the mantel, lighted it, and impudently offered one to the raginc, man on the 0 , 1 other side of the fireplace. Low had known the lust of murder, and he felt its old promptings in his heart then. It would have been an easy matter to seize the poker and dash out the other's brains as he sat there imperti- nently and vulgarly consuming his whisky and cigars; and he had been blackmailed so persistently since the trial of Martin Fenwick that he would willingly have put an end to it all by another foul crime. But the secret of Squire Fenwick's death would not even then be dead. There was yet the old woman who had made herself safe by confiding in her son. , Low scowled at his visitor for a moment.
"Well, bow long do you propose to stay ? " "You can answer that best," said the other,
'hl suppose you've been fledged at the Hopetown vulva, and I've got to make the thing good, is that it ?."

"The disposal of a gentleman's own money is nothing to do with any other gentleman, isit ? I haven't been spending your money, 'ave I, eh ?" It suddenly struck him that he had been sayino that which had double truth in it, and he laughed heartily at his unintentioned wit and helped himself to more whisky. Low saw that it would be of little use to continue his baulking tactics. Moreover, as his choler died down, he suddenly, remembered a plan he hbid co4itated upon earlier • in the evening, an under- taking he had determined to carry out himself. Parr was the very man for the undertaking. "Listen," he said. "You want fifty rounds. What do you say if I make it a hunched and litty?

"Wot do I say?" replied the other, craftily. "Why, that you'll want more than a hundred pounds.' worth of worl done for that extra hundred." ',You're not willing to earn that amount? " "I am, But I want to know 'ow it's to be done first."

' Well, it's like this. You see, this is a tine, dark night, or vill be when the moon gore in a few hours' time. What a splendid sight a good fire would make. You understand?" "Yes, 1 know. Ineendiarism. Ten years"are. Not me. That fifty quid will last me a bit. iest 'and it.over and I won't worry. Your schemes are too advanced fer me, Mr. Low. I've never done mere than six lilontlis at a stretch."
Yu needn't. be caught-. you fool! Come, I'll main. it two hundred in all: Just have another drink Bud think it Gver."

If lioaglas Low thought that by plying his Tisihr: with Ythkky he would beniuddle hifn into neguielieenee he had made a mistake. Parr was too frequent a r44itor to the public-house to sw•cumb rer..dily to the libations Low pressed upon him. Gradually the. terms rose, and Parr's eyes flftslyed at the prospect as Low at length reached I brce 1 undri d )xiunds.

-"I'll do it," finally cried the other. "By gad, I'll do it I Where's the place ? Low lowered his voice, though there was no need ror it, the servants' having long retired to rest. "You know the new. granaries that have be= built at the Barton?" "Yes," "They are easy to touch off, eh t• "Yes. But—*

_ "Never mind my interest in the matter," interrupted Low, guessing thp character of Parr 's expostulation. "Will you do the job 1" "Money down ? " "Half to-night and half to-morrow morning, pro- viding you make a good job of it." "It must be done to-night?" "Or to-morrow night. But you might as well do it now, while you are in the humour tor it." "I'll start straight away. Make your money over and in half-an-hour's time look out for tt, flare."

"You have' forgotten the moon. You nad better stay here till it is perfectly dark." They sat and talked, and drank at intervals, till Zeke Parr's face was flushed and his hot, gipsy blood was fired to the deed he had in hand. Then when the clock pointed to three Low counted over the notes that were to be Parr's due for the night's evil work, added them to the blackmail, lo demand which the crippled rascal had. made his late call at the Chase, saw the bribed incendiary through the French windows that led to the lawn, and closed them softly behind him. An hour later Low, watching from his bedroom window, saw a handful of red sparks flick against the black sky over against the Barton. Then a handful more and yet another, then a red flame shot up a couple of yards and before it had died away a glaring shaft burst out. Within five minutes the whole building was in a blaze. "Another stroke accomplished," he said. "Nothing can save either building or crop. The old man will be on his hands and knees now. And then, my haughty Grace, we will see how long this mock devotion will last."

Douglas Low was not the only one to see that first bright column of flame shoot up into the night blackness of the night. For from the gateway of a little cottage, bought with hush money, the price of a human neck, Ezekiel Parr, with his hands. stuffed into his pockets, clutching ,the banknote made over to him by Low, looked back upon his vile handiwork. lie smiled grimly. "You've had a fair innings against me, old Hendon," he muttered. "Many a seven- days' have I done through your reckoning up. I always owed you a grudge, and now I've paid it off with a bit of interest."

There pas yet another who witnessed that first glow of ruin. Grace Hendon's ivy-covered window looked across to an angle of the new barns. The fierce light of the fire played upon the walls of her room. She wakened with a start, and looked out. Then a startled scream escaped her. "Father!" she cried. "Father ! The new barns are on fire."

In a few minutes everybody on the farm was aroused, and they rushed hither and thither with buckets of water—an utterly ineffectual proceeding, whilst a horse was saddled and a messenger despatched to the nearest town for a tire-engine. An hour later the engine arrived, but the new barns and a thousand pounds' worth of newly threshed wheat grain were a charred and ruined heap. Farmer Hendon was bowed to the earth by his loss. While he had fancied there was the slightest hope of saving the granaries he had worked like a Trojan. But when every effort had proved fruit- less, and the brigade had added to the ruin by sogging everything with water, he reeled back into the house a ruined, broken-hearted man. "Father!". His daughter's soft arms were about his neck, her sweet breath was upon his temples. "Father, dear, bear up. It might have been some worse calamity." "My child," he said, "you do not know what this loss means to us. More than you imagine. Not one pennyworth was insured." • "Why I thought you wrote the letter, and sent the money away the day before yesterday." "I intended doing so, but as I was going down to the village to post I, met Mr. Low, and he advised me differently. Re had a customer, he said, who would buy the grain' and he suggested I should defer insuring until I had my barns empty for a day or two, and save the extra expense. It seemed wise advice."
"It was cruel," said Grace. "Did this customer call? "

"No; he was to come with Mr. Low to-morrow. And now a thousand pounds' worth of grain gone in one night These farm buildings are heavily mortgaged, my dear. The interest on the mort- gage comes due next week and I haven't a penny to pay it with. That wheat was my only salvation. It would have helped me to clear not only a year's interest, but would have wiped a hundred and fifty pounds off the capital." Farmer Hendon refused to be comforted, and sat in the old armchair in his kitchen corner, a dis- consolate and ruined man. The outlook was the darkest that had ever faced him in a calling which, more than most others, yields most capricious satis- faction for time and labour expended. Grace cheered him as best she could, assuring him of her love ;but her father, honest and discerning mau as he was, believed her own assumed good spirits to be due to a want of conception of the enormity of their loss. Grace left him at length and went to her room, trying to straighten out the perplexing thoughts that crossed her mind, thoughts of the two strange mysteries that had brought such misery into hes life, for no apparent purpose, the mystery of the murder and the later one of the fire.

div.head: CHAPTER /X. •
div.p: CHAPTER /X. •
IN 1108PITAL.

No punishment more hopelessly useless could have been given Martin than that of grinding out a number of revolutions a day on the crank, for the work accomplishes nothing other than the record- ing, by an automatic device, of the number of turns. Long before he had finished an hour's labour his hands were blistered by the rough handles, and his back and shoulder-blades ached with the unac- customed and awkward occupation. But this was not the worst. As the day advanced a trembling like the ague took possession of him. From time to time a cold sweat broke forth from every pore. His brain became dizzy, and he paused again and again, gasping for breath. The break for dinner gave him a brief respite, but he could not eat the wretched meal of skilly which was brought to his cell. But he gained a short rest, and at the hour for the re-commencement of labour took up his task again and turned at the handle. He knew then that he was unwell, that a fierc,e fever was burning in his blood. His lips were welled, yet he would not ask for water; though he died under the fierce strain he would not appeal to the doctor. His manhood resented asking the slightest favour in a place like that. He had not turned off four of the seven thortsamt revolutions ordered; when at length nature broke utterly down. A warder who looked in to inspect his work found him lying on the floor in a dead faint.

"Hullo,' he said. "What's this? filhammin' already ? " Martin never heard.him, but a moment later a torrent of water deluged him from hgad to foot, and with a painful shock his senses suddenly returned to him. _ _ _

"Ah I " said the warder, with a chuckle. "I thought that would brim, You round. Now then, up you get, will you, and hurry up with that seven thousand. Iloilo, what's this ? Only four thousand turned off? Come on, now, unless you mean to 'pack up your box ? ' . And if that's the, game let us know, and we'll try another." Martin had heard this phrase "pack up your box" used by a warder before, and he understood its meaning. A lag who meant to "pack his box" was one who had determined to resist all authority, who had got a heavy fit of the sulks and had deter- minedly struck against work. The penalty for such an offence was heavy. It meant the dark cell at the very least, or a dose of "No. 2," by which the "cat" was designated in prison parlance. Faint though Martin was ho managed to stammer out: "No, no, sir. I am ill; really, I am ill. I cannot work."

"Yes, I dares," hissed the warder, with a leer; "too ill to work but not too ill to put in your five eggs jn the yard yesterday. I heard what you said, mad make this place a. hell on earth for you, you see if I don't. You'll be glad to follow No. 48. Get up there, I say, and he planted a brutal kick on Martin's side.

The prisoner made a poor attempt to rise, but fell to the floor again, and the man began to wonder whether he had not perhaps gene a little too far. Kicks have a nasty knack of leaving bruises, though a warder's explanations easily outweigh a convict's charge, even when wounds are brought in evidence. "All right.," he said. "I suppose you want to see the doctor, eh? Well, you can't. lie won't be round again to-day, and I'm not going to fetch

PIM 11•••••••1Ki him specially for you. bo you can go on witn rug shamming. I'll take care to report you if rug wOrk'ain't finished; you mark that." Ranging the door behind him, the warder left the cell, upon the floor of which the tortured victim lat, in a second swoon. But at supper a different warder presented llistm self with the meal, and found Martin still 1,0.6.. unconscious on the ground. Though he, too, had we invariable suspicion that the priconer was share" ming, yet he deemed it the wisest course to send for the doctor. When that official appeared he Pot at a glance that Martin was seriously ill. Restore" fives were quickly applied. "How long has the prisoner been like this?" he asked, when at length Martin had returned to consciousness and had been placed upon his bed. "Why, the man is in a most dangerous conditic It's a bad attack of rheumatic fever. Remove hi to the hospital at once." Dr. Gibson superintended the removal personally, and saw that the patient was properly cared for The fever had taken a firm grip of him, and IV days he lay upon his bed fighting a fight of life at death. At times he was delirious, and then ' sweet phantasy of his younger years recurred him. Once more he was in the meadows wi Grace and Douglas. Once again they played, so' romped, and fought and made it up again as yore. Once more the hallucination of the moi recent happy days possessed his brain, and: would clasp his lover in his arms and print lu after kiss upon her sweet lips. And then even he held her she would seem to lose substance are become a mere shadow, and the shadow would flu away beckoning to him as she went, and with ope arms he would pursue the shadow crying aloud. "Grace, my Grace," until at length he would rega• his ,consciousness and see the small windows of hospital and realise once more that he was in prisu. and that he was a murderer in the sight of the law, who had himself hung over the precipice of deg/ by the very skin of his teeth, and who was n 4 deemed fit or worthy to be at liberty among fellows.

And then again the sweet (lelirium. .Sp the . raged until at length the doctor declared all dani to be past. But it was not for many weeks aft' wards that Martin was able to leave the'frient precincts of the ward and go back to the darkne and degradation of the regular cell life. Duria. those days of convalescence he had many a frienit chat with his fellow lags, and heard many a story of sorrow and shame, of the bright hopes youth blasted by a single sin ; many a story, tL of manhood demoralised and degraded by the associations of prison life under a system t' knows no difference between the hoary-he offender who has spent the greater part of a li) time in prison and the young and susceptible sixty who has broken his heart and his parents' also an indiscretion that has pluaged him into _a I companionship for years, and made iipermara criminal of him.

Back to the cell again. The okler struck hoi to his heart, for the ward-room had been a vi able heaven to him with its special food, its , tically unlimited conversation, its light, , warmth, its freedom frorn'the galling, dog-li commands of the warders, its absolute rest.

So great indeed had been the transition that . the first wild ravings of his illness he had elm forgotten that lie was a prisoner, and felt like free man aid a human being again. It had heaven after hell; now it was hell again. The cnmk, at the doctor's instance, had not t re-enforced, nor was he again put on spec offenders' diet. But the old melancholy. routii the oakum, the dreaded monotony, the brain rott were his once more. He sometimes thought, however, that the f( had saved him, saved him from a madness than death, for it enabled him to tide over a 6. two months of the hateful nine months' probate And one day after he had been back his cell a little more than a month, a suddenly entered at an unusual hour. "Now then, No. 35," he'said. "Get your trig). together and pack up." At last he was to be moved. What was to bg, his destination ? To which of the penal establish:, ments was he to be taken ? He heard in the room that there was far more variety in the ftla, convict life, with its daily round of reasonable ucct, pation, and its relaxation, to a considerable extegof during out-door •working hours, of the rule perfect silence. Yet little did he dream of troubles that the future held in store. to% That day, in company with five others, be taken to the railway station. The degradatioi his position had never so fully appeared to 121111 when chained to his fellows he had to niS 11.0liie -1# way between the shrinking crowds of passengers 1:.;' the station, and he was glad of Alm shelter of VA third-class railway carriage into which, in corap* with a couple of warders, the gang was speed hustled. No sooner was the train on the move, howeleerr; than the prisoners, by some unexpressed und standing, arrived at the conclusion that the rigowi of prison life were to some extent to be , ignore? during the journey, for first one, then anot broke silence and the warders made no 5ig05,.0 interference. Then it was that Martin heard their destination was Minewood, and his heart Po, a great leap, for he knew • that, the railway fr°,,,, Henlea to Minewood ran right through Fenwic% The train would pass not more than two Initial' yards from Farmer Hendon's farm. The thought that he might see Grace's and the home where his boyhood was spent, now by right, buoyed him up all through the and he feverishly waited in a state of it_ excitement for just this one bright ray of hapr nese to beam into his darkened life. At length the train ran into Penwiek atatiol9 Instinctively he drew back for fear of being though, had he realised it, no casual observer have recognised in the closely-cropped Cloven convict the sprightly young squire who had °- been such a popular figure in the neighbourhooaa A shriek of the engine whistle, and the traial off again. His place was in the middle of carriage, but he craned his head forward, h eagerly out into the bright sunshine beyond. Suddenly came an order which in one mono chilled him to the heart. The voice of the opposite was heard calling out' "Hi, you there, by the window, No. 162, pull them blinds down. There's too much g 'here. Yes, the middle one as well." No. 162, sitting close to the window, had 4 other thought but to obey. But the fatal order °- gone like a dagger-thrust to Martin's heart. could not bear to lose this unparalleled joy for sake of risking the warder's anger. "If you please, sir," he said, "might the be kept up two minutes longer. That's my home we're passing, and-- ' "Silence," roared the wardep. "Speak ant word, and I'll make it hot for you at the other, Your old home, is it? Well, I thought. there something special about it by the way yotr glaring out. But this ain't a pleasure - to go sight-seeing." Martin made no reply, but with downcast sat listless. He knew by insttnet when they passed Fenwick Barton, and he knew, too, thatlf. brightest vision his eyes were likely to beho many a long day had been wantonly denied to rio'"ti The vision had been brighter than he drei For at the gate by the railway crossing, waitiat the train to pots, had stood Grace tendon. div.p: hat the committe of the Pupil T3achers Classes would be only too :hanktul to c.,,et the Corporation net of that dilemma by ocoupN log the inEtitute mlraing and after- noon with pupil teachers' classes. He hoird Warring- ton was going to rise to her educational responsibilities' (Hear, hear.) He hoped the Corporation would welcome them into thrir technical school, and that they would consider it a great privilev to educate the future teachers of the town. (Ap PI Anse.)

, SPEECEL DY DR MISS Dr Moss, prior to distributing the prizes, delivered an address. They could not all receive prize', he said, but it was not always the boys who got the priz who turned out the most effective citizses. (Hear, hear.) There were special qualities necessary to get prz. They must have an intense memory fir words and they must " cram" themselves. P.— he was not convinced that the system of ectucatio, oas quite perfect. He had had a little experience ;nastnach tor the last thirteen years he bad taught many divinity students, amongst whom was a large sprinkling of ex-pupil teachers and certificated teachers. He was bound to say that they did not make the best students. There wine exceptions, of course, but taking the average of that class of divinity students he confessed that as a teacher he did not like them. They seemed to have learnt in the course of their training, a few things only. Their range of study was very narrow, and there was a great lack of mental a7ility. They seemed in :"pable of applying the mind to some Wally new problem, the power to deal with facts that had not been dealt with. He advocated a thorough drilling in English litretature as a wonderful help in exercising the mind. He was de- lighted to hear that they had a technical school in War- rington, bat he believed theywere still without a firs'-class high f chlol . Something of the sort was wanted in order to enable boys and girls who attended the elementary schools to continue their studiel and rise step by step to the universities. (Hear, hear.) He was not sure whether the religious bodies of the town ought not to take the foremost place in educational 'progress. He held the opinion that all studies led up to theology. He advised the pupil teachers to equip themselves as comtilf tely as possibl," and address them'elves to their work in the fear of God. (4131ause.)

div.head: PRIZE LIST.
div.p: THE PRIZE LIST.

The prize Us was as follows : First class Queen's scholarship examination, 1960 : Nelly Bayley, People's Colleee ; Ada L Cnrbett, Orford School—First celss Ootober exemination, 1900 Third yea-, Nelle Barley, People's College ; Ada L Cerbott. Orford ; Ethel Jones, People's College: Lilian Craik, Fairfield • Leuiaa Hosier, Fmrfield ; Nellv Long. bottom, Christ Church School, Latchford ; M Wilde, Wycliffe ' • Maurice Glover, St. Anne's Second year, Janet Bibby, St. ; Lilian Foster, St. Paul's •, Nally Gandy, St. Peter's; Mabel Bellwood, People's College ' • Maul Hudson, PS, NBy Walker, People's Cellege ; Agnes Wallinet Peonieni College ; Fanny White, People's College ; Mead Wood. Fairfield ; Echel Wetshv, Smith-street. Firs': yea., Rose Craik, St George's ; Mabel Eeeland, Wycliffe ; Ella Wilson, People'e College ; Wallace Gandy People's College; Robert Simpson, National. For general proficiency, Evelyn Arnold, St Anne's; ' Maggie Edgar, St Anne's; Mabel Sederland, Penketh. Special prizes were awarded as follows :—For com- position (given by the Rector): Senior, Lilian Craik; junior, Wallace Gandy. Prizes for masheinatice (given by the Rev Morley Stevensoo): Senior. Maurice Glover; junior, Maud Wood. Two prizes for French (given by the Rev John Yonee) : Senior, Leuisa, Hostler; junior, Gertrude Hudson. Latin prizo (given by the Piincipal) : Nellie G aide% The services of the Mayor and Dr Moss were acknow- ledged and the Rev Theodore Biehop was thanked for the use of the room on the proposition of the Rector. Alderman Momes in seconding the motion. ineteioned that the Technical Ineti'.ute Committee had made arrangements whereby the pupil teachers classes could be properly and efficiently carried on in the new insti- , A high grade schenl would also be made if circumstances seemed to justify it. Personally he thought there was a great want in the town for such a school. He knew of a number of boys who had to travel to Manchester and Liverpool in order to attain the necessary eiucation. He would only be too glad if the Council would place the money required at the dis- posal of the committee. • The Mayor in acknowledgine the vote said there was every disposition on the part of the committee to meet the committee of the centre in the meet favourable way possible, (Bear, hear.) They realised that it was the duty of the town as for as the law permitted, to use whatever facilities they bad at their disposal to further the great cause of education. (Applanee ) Warrington had become a county borough.* Under the new education proposals ef the government. Warrington would be constituted an educational authority. He did not know what form and powers the authority would have, but one thing was certain—that in all probability the control of all that ap Pertained to secondary education would be laid upon the Corporation in some way or another: The Corpora,- tion was willing and anxious to do all it could in this matter, but they must be prepared to face the Bill. Money would have to be spent. and spent liberally, but he believed it could net he better spent. (Applause.) Mr Moss and Mr Bishop also acknowledged the vote of thanks.

div.head: THAT "LITTLE DISH"
div.p: THAT "LITTLE DISH"

How we do like a little dish of something nice, served up hot! Charles Lamb would have sold his shirt for a tenser suckling pig done to a turn. Doctor Johnson used to say that a dish of tea was the most fragrant of life's beverages. "Why, what am I a-thinking of, I shall for. get my own name next," said Toby Veck, "It's tripe— the best tripe ever stewed." And his daughter Meg smilingly gave him the basket, in which reposed a hot steaming dish of his favourite meat. "My wife prepared nice dainty little dishes to tempt my appetite," said Mr Henry White, of that beautiful Devon town, Torquay, "but somehow I seemed to have lost all inclination for food, and after sitting at the table trying to swallow a little I used to say to her:— " ' It's no use. I can't eat it. You may as well take it away.' This sort of thing soon told a tale for one can' go without food for long without losing strength. See- ing my condition, a friend strongly advised me to try Seigel's Syrup. He said it had cured him, and might do me good. " My appetitelno longer needed!coasing. I could eat well-nigh everything that was put before me. Each dose seemed to give me life and vigour. To-day no matter what ails me, Seigel's Syrup puts me right." That " little dish," in fact is once again the favourite. " Some three months ago my wife got thoroughly:run down. For over a fortnight she could keep nothing on her stomach." Mr Henry White,"when certifying to the truth of this on September 13th, 1900, at his house, 10, Pediford Terrace, Torquay, Devon, does not say what was the matter with his wife.

We know why the " little dish "failed to digest, and we quote the words of the famous physician to prove it: "In the nervous and irritative form of dyspepsia, this is. a very prevailing symptom As is also a sensation of striking, as if the stomach required food, due to the fact that the food has left the stomach in a half-digested condition." Who could enjoy a "little dish," when the food could be but half-digested? "She was troubled a good deal with wind,and seemed to be losing her strength.l fetched a bottle of Mother Seigel's Syrup from Holloway's Drug I Stores,and she Comm T'lced taking it. In a short time she was quite well again." H'm, sime men would now sell their shirt for a bottle of this remedy. This essay, then, upon " little dishes" proves that while man and woman can in no wise always relish that favourite dieh, yet a cure is ready to hand. One that has served men and women alike for more than the past thirty years.

A Warrington Picture in London. Visitord to the Warrington Art Gallery may have recently missed the untioished picture of Vortuny's entitled, "Acrobats at Tetuan,' which was presen- ted to the town by Mr RJbert Davies. The explana- tion is that it hat been temporarily removed to London where it is included in the exhibition of Spanish art in the Guildhall, owed by the Lord Mayor of London on Monday In commenting upon the exhibition, a London correspondent writes :—"North-country galleries, and indeed mu- 1 nicipal collections everywhere, have been unable to furnish anything of importance beyond the inter- esting Fortany sent by the Corporation of Warring- ton. Nor have the Spanish pictures in the hands of private collectors in Lancashire and Yorkshire been laid under serious contribution, and it is not to be overlooked that in some instances the tussle for the possession of a Velesques between London and Glas- gow this season has been very real. There are con- tributions by the Duke of Westminster and the Duke of De•K onsbire, though in both instances I am under the impression that they are lent from their houses in town. The exhibition, be that aa it may is an important one, and will be one of the serious attractions of the Loudon season."

ARCHDEACONTMIOAND.DEN'S VISITA-

Churchwardens and Sidesmen Admitted to Office. Liverpool Cathedral Scheme. The New Burial Act. The Van. Arcncheicoe els Aden held a visitation at the Warrington Parish Church on Monday morning for the prover° of admitting to office the recently elected churchwardens and sidesmen of the district. Before commencing his formal charge the Archdeacon explained that the Rector of Werrington was not able to be present that morning as tie was with leis son at Maivern. Hl@ son returned from Lyda indisposed, and his father was with him in the hope that a ch inge might mean his clmplete recovery. The Rector had written a letter of apology for his abeence. Cantimuine, the A.rchdeamen sail they were all interested in that old Perish Church, for whiee an appeal had been iesued for its restoration. The Rector and wardens had put off making any large and expensive alterations in the church because of the necess- ity for an enlargement of the day schools of the town. Tiny had made an appeal for £3,000, arid it was not merely addressed to tee, people of Warrington, but to all in the neighbourhood who had the interests of the church at heart. He had no doubt that if they could in any way help the restoration of that historic church they would gladly do anything in their power. Proceeding with his charge the ARCHDEACON set forth the duties of churchwardens. Be coutinuel :—" As regards the services of the church, it is the duty of the warden& ro observe and report, but not to interfere with the Vicar or the. cervices. When he "presents" his com- plaint to the Bishop, he leas fulfilled his duty, and the responsibility to act rests with the Bishop. Very fre- quently, whoa any differences arise as regards Ritual, a triendly talk between Vicar and wardens may bring about an understanding on the subject,. After all the bulk of the clergy and of the laity are moderate and reasonable men, and are not factious or quarrelsome. There are other duties which appertain to your office. You are wardens or custodians of the property of the Church. The care of the church and churchyard de- volves open you. To you belongs the right of seating parishioners in their parish church, and the right also to assist the Vicar ire the distribution of alms. I think silver vessels ought to take the place of eleetro- plate vessels for Holy Communion. Silver vessels are much cheaper than in old day, and for His Holy Table we ought to provide the best. lam sure the Bishops would gladly receive contributions towards supplying silver vessels in the poorer churches." After alluding to the necessity for clean and decent sur- pliefie for choirs, adequate kneeling accommodation for the congregation, and ecrimu;ous cleanliness of churches the Archdeacon said i—" There is one other matter that I must mention. I hay.' heard that at the Easter veetries there has been some grumbling about" outside cellec- tiens." I hope a spirit of coneregationalism is net going to dominate our wardens. There is already to much of "My " church and "My "parish. We must ever keep in mind that we are members of one great Church, and that we have a duty to the one body as member, Our diocesan institutions, our local church charities are all languishing for lack of more financial help. The Bishop's Sustentation Fund for increasing the stipends of the clergy received one generous donation of £l,OOO in the past year, but more annual subscriptione are required. The Ceutch House. which will he formally opened on May 18th will soon bscome the centre of our diocesan organisations and cherities. The day cannot be far distant when the new cathedral will rear its lofty towers and graceful spires above the great and growing city of Liverpool. In that day shall all men know that the diocese of Liverpool has ceased to be a number of isolated parishes, but has bec )me a united and solid fisree making for righteousness and peace and goodwill a =eget men. The enthusiasm, the perseverance, the sacrifice, which will imitate and bring co parfeation so noble a monument of Christian veital an conspicuous generosite cannot pass away with its accomplishment, but they will remain the heritage of her eons for generations to come. At the present man:sent I can only speak of the progress of the Oath°. dial scheme in•general terms. The provisional com- mittee are at work and already several donations of £lO,OOO and others ranging from £l,OOO to £5 000 have been promised. The Lord Bishop, or Sir William B. Forwood will be glad to receive donations, and the oommittee agree that the subscription may be spread over five years. The public appeal will be made in a few weeks, but on issuing it we are anxious to be able to show a substantial amount of supped: The Bishop has appointed a cemniission to consider the complex quetition of church accommodation, church district, church removals, and church vicarages. This commission will consist of the two archdeacons, the rural deans, and ten laymen elected by the ten rural deaneries. Just twelve years ago, such another com- mission made its reports to the late Bishop, and as a result certain churches were removed, new churches were built, and the boundaries of ecclesiastical districts were re-arranged. But many of the recommendations could not be carried out owing to the opposition Some- times of the patron, sometimes of the people, Some- times of the vicar, and sometimes of all three. In several cases the oppesition wai just and reasonable from the parochial opine of view, if not from the diocesan, lem sure the commission will lee glad to re- ceive any helpful facts, or useful information from those concerned. We want light on the whole question. and we look to the church wardens as practical men to forward us facts and figures and practical suggestions. It is the determination of our Bishop to do all that is possible for a Bishop to do, to provide for the spiritual wants of the flock, over which the Holy Ghost has made him overseer. On the Ist January this year the new oßurial Act became the law of the land. This Act applies to burial grounds provided by local authorities,7and not to old parish churchyards. Nevertheless it demands the care- ful stony of the clergy and wardens. The Act was the ;outcome of the report of a Seteet Committee presented to the House of Commons in 1898. This committee was representative of Churchmen and the Nonconformists, and it.contained men as far avert politically and eccles- iastically as Mr Carve Williams and Lord Cranhourne. The report was unanimous, and the Act embodies the compromise arrived at. If parts of this new Burial Act seem unjust to Churchmen we can only plead thee our representatives erred on the right side—on the side of Christian charity—rather than give any occasion for unhappy differences between Christian men over the burial of their deed. The main features of the Act are :—(1) The re-distributino of powers, duties and functions between the Seeretary of State and the Local Government Board. The Secretary of State will he the central authority regarding the consecration of trarid! grounds, the allottment of parts thereof for the USO of particular denominations, the building of chapels, and the removal of human remains ; and new functions are entrusted to him with respect to the fixing, varying, or commutation of, or compensation for, fees payable to minisiters of religion, ecclesiastical officers and sextorie. It will be observed that, speaking generally, all ceiestions relating to sanitation, and to the constitution, powers, and finaucies of burial authorities, will in future be dealt with by the Local Government Board, whilst matters affecting the interests of the church and other religious denominations and their officers are referred to the Secretary of State, whether such matters arise in connection with burial grounds under the Burial Acts or with cemeteries under the Public Health (Inter- ment) Act. (2) Consecration. Under the Burial Act. 1853,a portion of the burial ground must be consecrated Under the Public Health (Interment) Act 1379, no por- tion need be consecrated. Hence difficulties aroie with burial bodies about consecration, and a few BLitinps ." dedicated" the portion ailetted for the burial of Churchmen, but "dedication" could not be an equive- lent for "consecration" from a legal point of view. Only by a "sentence of consecration" could the ground ,be preserved for ever for sacred purposes. The first I section of the new Barial Act sets out the law which will lin future regulate the consecration of burial grounds. (3) Cemetery chapels. The law relating to cemetery chapels is entirely altered by Section 2 of the Act, as far as relates to chapels to be erected hereafter. All burial authorities will have power to erect on any part of their ground which is not consecrated or allotted as above a Chapel for the performance of burial Services ; but such a chapel must he unconsecrated, and for the use of all denominations in common And if any part of the ground is consecrated or allotted to any particular denomination the burial authorities may be called upon by the Secretary of State to cause or allow a chapel or chapels for funeral services according to the rites of such denomi- nations to be erected, furnished, and maintained on the site or sites so appropriated. Such chapels will be erected furnished, and maint aired at the cost of persons belonging to the particular denominations, and residing within the district of the burial authority. The obliga- tion hitherto attaching to burial authority, whit, have provided a cemetery under the Public Health(lnterment) Act, to build a chapel at their own cost in the conse- crated part, if any, will cease. This alteration in the law will throw upon Churchmen in the future, the whole cost of building a chapel in the consecrated por- tion of the burial ground ; or it may lead them to make use of their parish churches for funeral services and so dispense with the necessity of a cemetery chapel altoget- her. These are the more important sections of the new Act. If this Act wilt only enable us to get rid of the worst of all grievances—the sentimental grievance—if it will only deliver us in the future from so called " burial scandals" the text for many heated attacks on the Churnh—we will not have paid too dearly for it by the loss of certain privi:eges enjoyed by Churchmen under previous Acts.

THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

Thursday's opening ceremony was chiefly confined to the ladies. A lady in the person of Miss Bessie Dutton oceupied the chair,the tea ,sr was declared open by Mrs C E Parker, and the platform was occupied by most of the lady workera in connection with the bazaar. M.ss /lassie •Durrox, in the course of a few intrc- ductory remarks, asid it was a great pleasure to be there in the midst of that bright and beantiful scene. They could only speak of a very old institu on when they came to speak of bazaars. In her opinion they always brought a brightness and freshness with them. It was a very good thing to have something bright. In their church life they wanted something light and cheerful and she thought a bazaar did supply a great deal of that. The power of their platform at such ceremonies as those depended upon who was on it. (Hear, hear.) Mrs PARKER said it WAS a great pleasure to her to he ' here and to receive such a very kind welcome. She always felt as though she had been associate with Bewsea -road Church all her life because one of her earliest recollections was collecting for it and bele." present at the foundation stone laying. (Hear, bear,) Although a small child at the time she remembered go- ing with a number of little ones to lay their contribu- tions on the foundation istones. Mr Berry afterwards presented each of them with a purse with their names inscribed, and it was one of the greatest treasures she had. She would like to say a word of congratulation upon the beautiful decorations at that bazaar. She did not think she had seen anything more effective. It was ' a happy thought to have hit upon a British Empire bazaar just at this particular period. Perhaps the British Empire owed more to Mrteodism than was usually recognised. (Hear, hear.) Every force that made for righteousness and tended to build up the morel life of the people was a great gain to the whole nation, and therefore in doing what they conic! for (ha maintenance of the Bewsey-road Chapel they were Simply following the lead given to them by their great founder John Wesley. (Hear,hear.) Then in addition she understood they wished to help Silver-st. School. Every man and woman must realise the importance of their day school work. The girls and boys of to'day would soon be our men and wonoen;and it was of the utmost Importance that we should do everything in our power that they should grata into useful men and women. (Hear, hear.) Unfortunately many of them were de- prived of their natural advantages. In their social con• ditions they were quite unable to have the cares which we bestowed upon our little ones, and therefore the day school was often their one chance in life. When we realised this we felt bound to see to it that our day schools, both in equipment and teaching staff, were as efficient as it was possible for them to make them. (Hear, hear.) With two such objects—and she supposed one or two minor ones—they must feel impelled to make it a success, and she sincerely truate 1 that the B wsey-road friend' would have the pleasure of realis- ing the sum of £l.OOO, which they hoped for. She had pleasure in declaring the sale open. (Applause). The Rev C U HOCKEN, in acknowler.ging the services of Miss Dutton and Mrs Parker paid a graceful tribute to their eloquence, and proceeded to state that they made an excellent bevinning on the previous day. They found that the total receipts on the first doy were between £350 and £4OO. (Applause). If they could maintain the high level of the preview; day they could see their way to a satisfactory termination of their efforts. (Applause). Two prettily attired girls then stepped forward and presented Miss Dutton and Mrs Parker with beautiful bouquets. The gifts were acknowledged and the sales then coin- meoced.

Return of the Torpedo Boat Destroyers. Toe flotilla of torpedo boat destroyers left lien- cheater on Monday afternoon for Kingstown, and their departure was witnessed by a large number of citizens. The destroyers passed through Latchford Locks shortly after foul- o'clock, and despite the fact that the weather was somewhat unfavourable, Ihundreds of people had assembled. The flotilla which was divided into two sections was headed by the Leven. Four destroyers were in the large lock at the same time—probably for about 20 or 25 minutes—and the public had thus an excellent opportunity of seeing these remarkable warships. When the water had been lowered to the necessary level the boats left the Locks at a good speed, and , were soon lost to sight. The remaining boats were 'dealt with in exactly the same manner.

The following statement was made by Mr. C. F. LECTURE AT WARRINGTON ON SOUTH AFRICA.

"South Africa: A trip to the seat of War" was the subject of a lecture, with animated pictures and music delivered in the Parr Hall, Warriogton on Monday even- ing by Mr D h Salmond, .of Gissgow. The proceeds were in aid of the local war fund, bat owing to the small attendance :his fund will not appreci- ably benefit thereby. Toe Mayor (Alderman Roberts) presided, and he was accompanied on tee platform by I the lecturer and Captain Waring, superintendent of the Warrington corps of the St. John Ambulance Associa- tion, the members of which association had made the arrangements. In introducing the lecturer,his worship said he under- stood the lecturer came from Scotland,and he was abont to say he would educate them that evening, but he did not think that was necessary on the question of the war in South Africa. Perhaps they knew as much about it, —be was going to say as much as they cared—but they knew it was a war that had special interest to then& because a large number of their fellow-townsmen were doing duty in South Africa. (Applause.) He c mgratu- lated Mr Salt:load on coming from, perhaps, one of the best municipally governed towns in the United Kingdont, namely, Glasgow. But that was only by way of paren- thesis. Ele was glad to have an opportunity of paying him, as a citizen of that great city that well- lessrved compliment. When their first detachment volunteered for active service and were accepted by the G Ivern- ment they went out under the promise that their wives and children stionld be cared for during their absence. That promise was repeated with regard Cu the other reservists and the various sections of the Volunteer core panies, who had gone out, and the promise held good that day. His fellow-townsmen hed responded most generously to the calls which had been made upon theaa to carry out that promise, and he bad no fear that then* would be a failure on the part of anyone. (Ilear,hear.i The object of tne lecture was to supplement the ttinde whist were necessary for the purpose he had named and he was glad to take that opportunity, perhaps the only one that would be afforded him that night, of ten dering his thanks to Captain Waring, and those associated with him, for having taken the trouble and accepted the responsibility of arranging for the lecture (Applause.) . .

LE6TIIIIER, at the outset, said it was not man; years .go when Africa was comparatively unknown ta them, but it had been a great Cell in their thoughts during the past two years, and many parts of it were exceedingly well known to all of them on account of the various battles which had been fought and the , movements of troops which had been described from day Ito day in the newepapers. They had, in fact,a pathetic interest in the war, which they „tall regretted was still lingering on. He did not think they understood the terrible nature of the war, certainly to the fullest extent until their beloved Queen died. Sne had had her heart wrung,by the loss of her grandson, Princo Christian Victor. Their interests in Africa were many and varied and whatever their opinion might be about the war there was no doubt that he had never yet met a person who was willing for Great Britain to give up Small, Africa. That was impossible if they wished the British Empire to hold together. The Caps was the keystone of the arch on which the empire rested, and their responsi- bilities to the settlers were so great that they could not give up the Cape. (Applause ) The lecturer stated that he and his wife some years ago made an extensive tour in South Africa. and visited most of the battlefields. His description of the towns, habits of the people, and the country were listened to with interest. The lecture was illustrated by a series of 150 beautiful views kindly lent by Sir Donald Currie. A pleasing break in the lecture was the rendering of "The Village Blacksmith" by Mr Salmond, who is the possessor of a rich and well-trained voice. Portraits were shown of Kruger. Sir Alfred Milner, Mc Cecil Rhodes, and several of the G-nerals. while with the kinema"ograpti 'views were given, amongst others, of the launch of the R.M.S. Bram:flat Castle, loading cargo, passengers embarking at Southampton, visitors promenading on deck, Lord Roberts inb irking for the Cape, Royal Caledonian Hos- pital boys, with piper on deck ; TantalLm Castle in Channel, tugs in heavy coa at Durban, street in Cape- town, rickshaw race, train crossing the veldt, ambu- lance corps at work, Mr Kimger driving in Pretoria, arrival of Lord Roberts at Capetown, train crossing Forth Bridge,and a street in Johannesburg. Captain WartiNa proposed a hearty vote of thanks to . Mr Salmond for the able manner in which be had enter r tamed the audience. i The vote was carried with loud applause. ; Mr Sausiositi, in returning thanks, said it bad given ; him very great pleasure to come to Warrington. He , also added that ho had raised over £2,000 this season by , lecturing for war funds. (Applause.
