div.head: Rev. W. A. Knight's Farewell
div.p: The Rev. W. A. Knight's Farewell
Sermon.

The Rev. W A Knight, curate of St. Ann's Church, Winwick-road, who has been appointed curate bf St. Cnad's, Derby,preached his farewell sermon at St. Ann's Church, on Sunday evening to a large congregation. Before commencing his discourse, he said he wished to take advabtage of that opportunity to thank all the kind ifriends at St. Ann's for the sympathy they had given to him since he came to the parish. A little sympathy to a parson went a long way in his ministerial life, because after all, a parson was a man. He wanted , sympathy and love. Might he ask for that sympathy 'to be extended to the clergy of the parish. A little practical sympathy also was a great help to the clergy and wardens when the bag want round on that and sue- needing nights. He urged them to do their level best to:belp on God's work in that part of His vineyard. In interesting gathering took place in the St Ann's Mothers' Meeting tt Winwick-road, on Monday afternoon, when presentations were made to the Rev W A Knight. The gifts which were presented on behslf of the donors by the Rev James Davies (vicar) consisted of a very handsome kit bag fitted with solid brass mounts, a purse of gold and an illuminated address from the congregation and choir and a silver inkstand from the mothers of St Ann's Mr Davies said that the pulpit of St Ann's Church would always be open to Mr Ko,ght whenever he visited or was near Warrington and expressed a hearty desire that he would avail himself of the privilege at no distant crate. Mr Knight briefly returned thanks. Buckley-street RS A. Society.
The *thrive society whicti. h.s now a memher.hip ol
about 200, cekbralled RS third anniversary on Sunday.
Tte R,rvicie in the morning was conduct-ed by Cour]. Walter Brouoh,whore efforca were highly appreciatiA. A
sp.cial feature of the afternoon proceedtn,s was the

visit of the members of St Peter's Bible Class. The chair was taken by Mr Thomas 8 Steel, who in the course of a brief address expressed the pleasure it gave him to see such a eneness of feeling existing between the members of St Peter's Bible Class ani the Buckley- street P.S.A., and congratulated the men upon the brotherly spirit exhibited by them that afternoon. Toe Rev II U Roberts gave an address upon the words "iSet k in the broad places thereof if ye can find a man." Dating the afternoon the Legh-street Quartet Party gave two pieces, entitled" Come unto me" and " The Mane Fisherman's Evening Hymn," and they were well received. Mr F Prycejones sang two solos, "The Children's Home," and" Thl Better Land," and he was also much appreciated. The fine voice of Mr R Cook was heard to advantage in a contralto solo. Mr A Trow accompanied with his usual ability. In the evening the pulpit ma occupied by Mr Charles Roylance (01 Moore), whose efforts were welcomed by a large congre- galon. Daring the evening Madame F Christian rendered a solo in a feeling manner. Special anthems were given during the day by the choir, whose sing- ing is deserving of much credit, and the conductor, Mr W Richardson, is co be congratulated upon the efforts put forward by him to ensure the success of the choral Part of the services. ' Wycliffe Sunday School Anniversary. This auspicious event in connection with Wycliffe Sunday School took place on Sunday and the high standard of previous years was well maintained. The , preacher for the occasion was the Rev Professor Armit- age, M&., of the United College, Bradford. Be based his morning discourse on the text. 11 There is a lad here, which bath five barley loaves and two small fishes : butlwhat are they among so many ?" John 6 e., 9 V. The discourse was addressed principally to teachers and Christian workers. He referred to the miracle of feeding the multitude as being typical of Christ's bands laid upon human weakness and assured all workers for Christ that with Big mighty hands laid upon them their efforts would meet with a succeSs which was beyond their anticipations or reckoning. Special hymns were sung, the singing being heartily joined in by the Sunday school

Have we at last lumped on a genuine cure for over- indulgence in alcohol? We are, like Agrippa, begin- ning to believe it after reading the remarkable htochure issued by the Tacquaru Co., 12, Noel olk-street, Strand. This proves, on excellent testimony, that the Tacquaru treatment succeeds in ninety-seven cases out of a hundred. The Faculty ac- knowledges itself amazed at the marvellous success of this new remedy, which destroys the taste for alcohol and kindred drugs, making them absolutely ab- horrent to the patient. Certainly, with three hundred publicly-tested cages, Tacquaru seems worthy of imme- diate inquiry. We warmly recommend the perusal of this little work (which is sent post free) to any f ainily circle suffering from the vhie that is sapping the nation's vitality. A strong point about this proved mire is that it can be taken as ordinary medicine, and in no way in- terferes with general habits, while the inebriate home becomes practically a thing of the past.—" Whitehall Review."

Union of Lancashire and Cheshirelinstitutes.l The ordinary monthly meeting of the council was held on Tuesday, at the Memorial Hall, Manchester, Mr W T Postlewaite presiding. It was reported that 52,940 papers had been requisitioned by the institutions, as compared with 50,90.5 in 1900, and that 41,431 exercises had been sent up, as against 37,668 in the preceding year. The Results of the Labour Examination.

..--..—. .. - Mr William Jones, the school attendance officer, has received the following results from his Majesty's Inspector of the recent labour examina- tion at Warrineon. of the five candidates pre- sented for examination in Standard IV., four passed. Seventy-seven were examined in Standard VI, 25 passing and 52 failing, while in Standard VII. four candidates passed out of the 10 that were examined.

THE programme has The National Liberal been issued of the Federation. annual meetings of the liational Liberal Federation to be held at Brad- -I°d the 13th, 14th, and 15th of this month. At the great public meeting in St George's following the usual sessions of the Council, Sir 11 CAMPBELL- 450.NELNAN is to be the chief speaker, and a long array of Liberal members of Parliament will be Present. The principal resolutions to be submitted at the Council meetings, comprise a general de- claration of adherence to Liberal principle, con- demning the means used by the ministerial candi- dates to secure a ietory at the last general elec- tion and pledging the Council to strenuous and aremitting opposition to the Government. This Is to be followed by specific resolutions on the ,growth of National Expenditure, Education, the and Laws, Housing of the Working Classes, tuPerance Reform, "One-man-one-vote,' the ,hg°use of Lords Veto, and London Governmect. here is a large body of prospective Liberal Legis- lation involved in these resolutions. On the ;sub- of South Africa, there need be no differences betaNgst Liberals on the terms of the motion to sh 'Proposed. It simply calls for a policy which 5)1 Secure a full measure of self-Government for 2(1 newly incorporated territories, equal rights to 'le white people, and just and humane treatment of the native races." Whatever views may be held
as to the origin and conduct of the War, Liberals

are in substantial agreement as to the necessity of a policy of pacification following these lines. The National expenditure resolution expresses appre- hension and alarm at the advancing expenditure and increase of the National Debt, and protests against " Money being squandered in doles to favoured classes of the community," and in par- ticelar against the renewal of the Agricultural Rating and Clerical Tithes Acts. Hereon not only will Liberals of all grades 'find common ground, but were such a resolution proposed in an °Pen public it would receive considerable support Oven from men who usually act with the Conserva- tive party. The resolution on National Educe tical expresses the belief that the " whole work of 13,nblie education ought to be entrusted in each district or area to some one responsible and popu- -1,845' elected body." As regards the Land Laws, taxation of ground rents and mining royalties, 6; tension of small holdings, and compensation for inlProvements, are the reforms demanded, the re- -3°lation being certainly marked by great modera- tion. Legislation on the lines of LORD PEEL'S Zeit is called for under the head of Temperance -°torni, and the usual registration and electoral iltc4rri which the Federation has advocated so 104 s g together with abolition of the LORD'S Veto, r-re declared to be essential to true Parliamentary f °Presentation. We sometimes hear it said that the 1,4111'113 Newcastle programme is dead, and buried. •out the effect has already been given to certain Of its proposals and here we have the main items Which are not yet embodied in legislation re- affirmed as still the active policy of the Liberal Party. Nor, except in the substitution for the Rome Rule resolution,—for which the time does nret seem opportune,—of a resolution in favour of htening parlamentary work by "A well-con- sred system of devolution," has that programme ever , lapsed. Its unrealised reforms are stout Plans of the Liberal platform at this day, and the Parts has never deviated from any of its basic „Principles, There are Liberals who hold that the 41. ational Federation, which at these annual meet- ings declares rather than discusses its policy, is neither representative or active enough to lead a g,reat Party to victory. In the "New Liberal "for May, Mr. J. H. YOXALL, M.P., under the head gg Liberal Re-organisation," criticises the Pederation's present organisation and:makes some Stiggestions for what may be called its reinvigora- tion, a first step to which, he suggests, would be Ivhat we may call the taking of a census of local Liberalism throughout the Country. These suggestions are well worth consideration in Coin- raittee, but not at the Annual Council Meetings of the Federation, which proclaim what a majority of the Local Associations have decided upon, and are pecessarily,therefore, more demonstrative than deliberative.

Much to their credit, the Miners' Federation, as such have endeavoured during the week to keep clear of the course which foolish and interested friends had marked out for them. tio far as could be gathered from th, reports of mass meetinks held in protest of the coal-tax, not a word was s•,id in favour of a cessation of work until the Chancellor of the Exchever withdrew the proposed duty. Some of the leaders, who had nothing to lose, but possibly something to gain, by a general strike, appear to be responsible for the excitement and th threatening attitude that prevailed. This was made fairly clear by the recommendation that the deci- sion should be referred from the delegates in London to the miners generally, which it was believed would culminate in a strike The miners have cer- tainly been advised that they will eventually te the real sufferers by the tax. But the majority were hard t,) convince, as well they might be,and had no intention of helping to pull the chestnuts out of the fire for the coal-owners. But even the majority felt the necessity of moving cautiously, as if they wer. ; but half convinced after all. Of course, they ought to hate seen that they were being made tools of, and that a general strike on such a pretence would be sheer folly.

Parliamentary journAlists say so little about the House of Lords that the series of articles on the subject now appearing in the " Empire Review" come almost in the nature of news. Every- one knows that the Lord Chancellor has no power of ciAling a speaker to order, nor of determining which shall have the ear of the. House if two essay to address it at the same time:and neither is inclined to give way. In recent years no trouble in this matter has arisen,noble lords having always shown their courtesy by deferring to one another. But Mr Thesiger, the writer of the article, mentions how a serious embarrassment occurred in the year 1847. Three lords clairrieu the right of oratory at the same time, and it was necessary to take a divi- sion in order to decide which should be heard first. In the final resort the maintainence of or&r in the Upper Chamber rests net with the Chair, but with the Assembly as a whole. Another peculiarity of the House often forgotten, is that the Laid Chancellor need not be a peer any more than a mayor need be a member of a Town Council. if, however, the Lord Chan- cellor be not a peer, he is not at liberty to address the House, but only to put motions. The Wool- sack is technically not in the house, though it is ' much forwarder than the Speaker's Chair in the Commons, and by a quaint custom, when the Lord Chancellor desires to take part in a debate, he leaves the Woolsack and goes to his own place as a peer." Then there is the curioal condition of things which prevails in regard to end:ng a sitting. Three members constitute a quorum, but there is no power of counting out th House such as the Commons possesses; and if the attendance were t ) fall below that number en any occasion, the Chan- cellor would have to remain sitting until other lords could be brought together to adjourn the House.

The extent to which the sugar tax will interfere with trade is now beginning to be felt. Perhaps the traders hardest hit will be the poorer class of confectioners, who depend almost entirely upon the sugar manufacture, and who, under the influ- ence of increased prices, find .their trade falling off at a time when their own liabilities have been augmented, and their customers, having, so many demands to meet, cannot afford to spend so much on what is regarded a 8 a luxury. . Another class of traders who will suffer are the restaurateurs. In all good restaurants the sugar basin is handed round for customers to help themselves at their ,own sweet will. For this no special charge is made. and therefore there is no convenient method of the purveyors recouping themselves for the additional outlay resulting from tie tax. There is not a sufficient quantity used to warrant an increase in the tariff of tea, coffee, puddings, and , other viands with which sugar is taken, and yet in the aggregate the restaurateur's bill for sugar must be a large one. On this he will have to pay the duty out of his existing profits. It is, therefore, a ease in which the impost does not reach the con- sumer, but is purely an embargo upon trade. The , people who suffer from the impost have, however, accepted the burden with a remarkable amount of resignation. A much larger interest is affected than is touched by the coal tax, though, perhaps, not as severely. So far, however, the only com- plaint has been in regard to the method of raising the duty.

Football has " fizzled-out " suddenly, and the excitements of a week ago have all vanished like a dream. The Warrington Rugby team has not come up to expectations, and the failure to secure either of the two Oaps competed for is a bitter disappointment. Such a chance of distinction as Warrington had last week-end does not come once in a decade, as a rule, but it was allowed to slip by, though not wilfully. That potent evil, " stage- , fright," plityed havoc with the Warringtonians, and they failed entirely to do themselves justice against the more experienced and wily cup-fighters of Batley. There was an immense exodus of people I from Warrington, but most of them suffered the added disappointment of being unable to reach the Headinglev ground in time for the match. It is a great pity that there is no redress to be obtained from railway companies in cases of this kind. The fight for the West Lancashire Cup on Monday re- sulted in a thaw, and as the close season has now arrived the right to the trophy will probably not be proved by either Warrington or Leigh this season. We shall have to solace ourselves with the milder delights of cricket for the ensuing four months, and there is no question about the fact that the change will be generally beneficial. Lan- cashire County Eleven, by the way, commence the season proper with a match on Monday at Ports- mouth against Hampshire.

The resolution of the London School Board not to ' appeal to the House o Lords against the decision in the Cockerton case, has had the effect of throw- ing the entire machinery of the educitional system of the country out of gear, except in regard to the most elementary subjects in day schools, and before work can be resumed on anything like a satisfac- tory basis, the spending powers of S3hool Boards generally must have a legislative definition. Owing to the congested state of Parliamentary business, Mr Balfour has declined to give any pledge that the new E location Bill of the Government will be introduced before Whitsuntide; though there is good reason to believe that it will be brought in previous to the holidays. Of course, the deadlock is one that calls for pr.,mpt legislative action, It was with a feeling of great relief that members of provincial School Boards received information of the intention of Ministers to take the responsibility for the situation on their own shoulders, The Government have a fine opportunity for reforming the educational system, and it is trusted they will so avail themselves of it as to render any further patchwork legislation unnecessary, in the event of their Bill passing, fora long time to come. But, if this is to be accomplished, tee public will have to be given time to consider the new proposals, and Ministers must be prepared to accept reasonable amendments. If this be done, great and beneficial reforms may be expected. There will not, however, have to be any repetition of the "take it or leave it" policy attempted six years ago, when practically the same Government endeavoured to re-arrange our educational establishments, aua failed. Other- wise the same results will assuredly follow.

Quite a stir has been male among the representa- tives of farmers in various parts of the country as to the milk standard they should adopt for recom- mendation to the Board of Agriculture. Dairy Farmers are divided between a desire to safeguard the public and at tne same time protect themselves. The Gloucestershire and Somersetshire Farmers' Society, for instance, have two standards before them one of w.iich was considered too low to pre- vent the possibility of adulteration, and the other was too high. It was pointed out by some of the members that a standard of 3.25 per cent. of fats would b practically unattainable, whiie it was admitted that with a 3 per cent limit a good deal of po ir milk would pass muster. The difficulty is th. great variation in milk itself, which arises from different causes, as the health of the cow, the breed the state of the land, and so on. It was, moreover, prove.' that the morning's milk is always of lower quality than that of the afternoon,and that in some c.Laes the former, although genuine, might have a difficulty in escaping suspicion of having been alultera',ed. Eventually it was decided to favour a pnsumptive standard of 3.25 per cent of fate, with a recommendation that every opportunity and facility might be given to suspected persons to show that their milk hail not been adulterated.

Should the account given in the "Daily Chronicle" be substantiated gas consumers and I users of electric power are alike on the eve of an enorm nis decrease of prices. the story is to the effect that" the gas itself is a coal gas, produced by forcing back coal gas obtained in retorts through 1 the coal in en incandescent condition, and the only residual obtain- d from this process is sulphate of ammonia which can be collected." It is also claioa- ed trial; the new gas supplies a cheaper mode of generating electricity. Toe cost of generation is now between a penny and twopence per unit. But with the Mond gas as a source of generation, it is I represented that the cokt per unit of electricity generated, including all cost of labour, repairs, &c . is less than one-twentivth of a penny per unit at the switchboard, and even that noes not allow full credit for the sulphate collected. Tie matter 15,01 colir,e,one in regard to which any other than expert opinion is valueless, but the man in the street can at least see that if this be true the public will not only have greatly reduced gas bills, but a reduction of tramway fares and an impetus given to all elec- tric extension,while the Corooration and companies who own electric undertakings will benefit to a story considerable extent. Let us hope the story •is not too good to be true.

Even the most sanguine of the promoters of the Glasgow Exhibition did not expect, probably, that everything would be in apple-pie order for the opening, It never is the case at these great exhibi- tions, and the fact that this one at Glasgow has been in" curl papers" all the week, to the time of opening, only proves it to be in the fashion. But once the doors are open, it is marvellous how rapidly the lee-way is ma le up. It is worthy of note, in view of the great pilgrimage from the Eng- lish provinces, that the electric tramway service in that gigantic and busy city had a week ago almost reached the point of completion. Some sixty miles had been converted to the purposes ot the electric installation, and the system is now perhaps with- out parallel in the whole kingdom. It may not be generally known that the tramway service in Glas- gow contributes largely to the relief of the rates. It is owned by the Corporation, and these substantial contributions are made notwithstanding che fact that for the halfpenny fare the individual passenger may travel a long distance. Some ot tie cars are not unlike Pullmans, and they follow each other with wonderful rapidity, t'Jus maintaining a perfect and continuous system of inter-communication be- tween all parts of the city that ranks next in size and importance to London. Their success is the more remarkable, since Glasgow has an excellent service of underground trains. But the halfpenny fare attracts cu:tom, and the result is that the Cor- poration. wise in its generation, is in possession of a magnificent asset, from the prAts of which it is possible to carry out vast schemes of civic improve- ment.

div.p: "A METHODIST OF THE METHODISTS."

The "Methodist Weekly" of the 25th ult.eontains an excellent photo of Mr R H Posnett, chairman of the Runcorn Urban District Council, together with the following reference .to his connection with a special :meeting, held the,. Brunswick Chapel, Moss-Oset, Liverpool; in connection with the Dis- trict anniversary of the Wesleyan Foreign .Mistioni: —" Thei Chair.nan was Mr Robert g Posnett, of Runcorn,, a Methodist of the Methodists, a son of the Rev Robert Posnett` and whose brother and sister are doing such grand service in the mission field in India. He is a J.P., by vinare of his office as chairman of the Runcorn Urban District douncil senior Circuit Steward (Runcorn). a local preacher and class leader. His first sentence rang clear and r true as he declared that all the blessings that had ever come into his life had come to him through his connection with Methodism, and what had been good for him he naturally believed would be go,KI for others. His experience of missionaries had neen this—they were the grandest heroes of the Church of Christ, and that in the highest and truest sense. And then a delightful piece of conceit pat the chairman and his audience on the best of terms, as he declared that he thought his brother to be the best missionary in the field, and that his sister was even better than he was—a sentiment Cue congrega- tioa cheered to the echo." CLAIM BY A GARDENER.

At the Widnes County Court last Friday before his Honour Judge Collier, Thomas Baldwin, market gardener, Upton Rocks, sued Edward P rcy.fariner, Widnes, for .E 9 10i. for bricks sold.—.lr Knowles appeared for the plaintiff, and defendant was re- presented by Mr F J Poole.—Plaintiff's case was that he owned a quantity of bricks at Penkoth on land belonging to the late Slr :Bolton. He sold a quantity of them to the defendant for a Later on defendant bought another lot for .C 1 103. Percy agreed with him at the same time to cart six loads of pipes from the same place at the rate of 44 6d a load. This left a balance of .£8 39. Defendant had often promised to pay him, but he had not done so.—ln answer to Mr Poole, plain. iff denied that the road on Nlr Bolton's land was bad The wheels did not sink up to the axle, and he did not agree with the defendant to repair the road for a sovereign —Sir Poole, for the defence, said there was an agreement on the part of Baldwin to pay defendant .E 1 for the repair of the road, as the owner had complained that a lot of damage had been done to it. He also submitted that 153 a load—and there were eight loads—was a reasonable charge for carting the pipes—The defendant was called and corroborated his solicitor's s'atement.—Lawrence Doyle and Richard Birch also gave evidence, the f u.mer stat- ing that the road was very bad, and he had had instructians to repair it. His Honour, in giving judgment, said that the amount per load was much t little. He would allow six loads at Os 61., which would reduce the amount of the piaintiff's claim to £7 lls.—Judgment was entered accord- ingly.

The Rev A Wells, deliv,sred his popular lecture on "Pompeii—the Buried City,"to a large and apprecia- tive audience, at Weston, on Wednsday evening. The lecturer was assisted by Mr J II Piekthall, as lantern manipulator and the whole of his valuable collection of GO slides were shown to advantage and considerably enhanced the lecture.—The chair- man was Mr F J Norman J.P., Beacom. and in an address he referred to the objsct of the lecture, which was to meet the expewee incurrel in having the W.-on Wesleyan C registered for the solemnization of marriages flitherto the Wesleyan community of Weston had been obliged to go to Runcsrn or elsewhere when they desired to be married in their own church. R iferring to the cordial relations which always existed between the late Canon Barclay and tee Nonconformist community, Mr Norm in remarked th .t Canon Barclay had once said it was all very well, but they (the Nonconformists) had to go to them to be married aud buried. Such things were, however, now changed, and thanks to the energy of the Rev A Wells, with the sanction of the trustees, all the important places of worship within the circuit would be registered for the solemnizetion of marriages, and they en- joyed already the advantage of the Burial Act. (Applau,e). —The esual votes of thanks were heartily accorded.

The one thing which is agitating the public mind is the trade depression Row being felt in the dir- trict. At Widnes things are bad, but are steadily improving: indeed, a converEation with one of the managers of an important works . there elicitPd the reassuring fact that they are not likely to go worse. Sa far so good. The prospelt in Runcorn, however, does not appear quite so bright, though here too, things are reported to be slightly improving and past the worst. Still there are far too many of our people "out of collar."

If what the people kay is true, that the census of Runcorn will show 17,000 instead of 20,000 (as expected) the position of the town so far as health statistics go is going to be altere I considerably for the worse? In past years we have palmed our- selves off as a remarkably healthy lot, but then 3,000 of an error ought to have some important bearing upon those delightfully deluding sheets medical reports. I by no means deride melical officers, or medical gentlemen, and am willing to admit they have their uses; but it does amuse me to 'see the charming way in which they make " figures from anything" when they get am mgst statistics. Southport has been doing the satre kind of thing,so perhaps we shall feels little consolation in having company.

The Runcorn Park now presents a very handlome awe trance, and is being greatly apprectve by the townen3ople. The numerous trees are already commencinF to bloom. The lake is daily a source of enjoyment, and affords no end of pleasure to the amateur yachtsman. It has also been stocked with fish-=--the gilt of an ardent admirer and follower of Sir Izaac. Now we have the lake, the fish, and the yachts ; who is going to send along the swans?

Information concertino, the transporter bridtze is being eagerly sough a.rer. Nothing authoritative however. seems fochcoming, and b yowl a rumour to the effect that the contract 4 are being considered we have to c Intent ourselves with conj-4cture as to when we shall enjoy our "mrial flight" over the Mersay.

We are to he given an opportunity of recognis- ing the valour of our " citizen soldiers " other than in the blatent uproar s 9 aptly express- ed in the word " Mafficking.' Indeed we have indulged too much in the abstract and now the Urban District Colwell are going to provide us with an opportunity of showing tangible recognition,it is to be hoped we shall respond hand- somely. At Frodeham the intention is to buy 14 watches, suitably inscribed and present them to all the" soldiers " there, and surely we will not be be- hind the villoge,

School Board s and things pertaining thereto are always acceptabl- to the Runcorn public; nod, especially so, to the Liberal section of the commu- nity, who by the way are face to face with the question of how to capture the odd seat at the next "call to arms." The question is one of vital importance and the earlier its "effect" is con- sidered the better will be the result. It is now intended that the Free Church Council, which is at length becoming an influence in the town, should join hands with the Liberal Executive and work stretiously to acquire its end. "Down with the rates!" was the cry which steered the voluntary school sup- porters to victory last time, awl it is with that mystic sentence that the ratepayers of Runcorn have to reckon, and will have to reckon. The pro- gressives would do infinitely well if they com- menced early and saw to their organization.

- On Sunday the missionary services were held in I connection withthe above place of vvorship,sermous being preache Iby :he Rev C L Cokrr, a coloured minister, of Sierra Leone, West Africa. The rev. gentleman came to England with the intention of b •coming a medical man, but he then decided to enter the ministry, and became a student at the Free Methodist College, Manchester. The services o were largely attended. The preacher, wh spoke p English perfectly, preached a sound and effective sermon. A. RuNrcoßN CAPTAIN'S NARROW ESCAPE

Further portim: trs of the loss of the Runcorn schooner CountesB of Carrick were gleaned from Thomas Williams, the captain, on his arrival in Runcorn on TharAsy: Williams, woo resides in Trentham-street, reported that he was bound from Bideford to Runcorn with 100 tons of china clay, and when cros +ing the Bristol Channel he was run down on Tassday by the steamship Rthelreda, of Whitby, of 3 000 tons, bound for St. Vincent. The steamer struck the scho)ner on ths starboard bow, euviou her down to the water's edge, and the vessel sank in about three minutes. The mate and an A.B. were drowned, and Captain Williams was picked up by the steamer in an exhausted con- dition, after floating about, on wreckage three- quarters of an hour. The collision occtirred seven miles off Baggy Point., and Captain Williams was landed at Penarth by a pilot boat. The Countese , of Carrick was owned by Mr 1 B Toft,_ of Runcorn.

ALLEGED Frisuos ON THE CORPORATION OF WIDNES. At the Widnes Police Coort on Tuesday before Mr B Brown. John Drury, book-keeVrt in the employ of the Widnes Corporation, residing at Ditton, was charged with feloniously and fraudulently embez- sling the sum of £ll7 19s fiat the property of the mayor, aldermen. sill burgess" of the said borough. Mr Craik, deputy town clerk, was present for the Corporation. and Mr Knowles defended. div.head: RUNCORN MYSTERY.
div.p: RUNCORN MYSTERY.
A Fireman's Sad Fate. Inquiry Adjourned. .

. . Coroner R Dobson opened an Inquiry at the Runcorn Police Court, on fuesday evening on the body of Patrick Tucker, second engineer of the as. Trafford. of Manchester, whose body was recovered from the Bridge- water Canal, on Monday afternoon. Mary Ann Tucker, of Kitchen-street, Liverpool. identified the body as that of her husband aged 30 years. She last saw him alive on Thursday morning when he went to his vessel at the Queen's Basin, Liverpool, and at thst time he said he hoped to reach Runcorn on S. turday. Henry O'Hare, 22, Lampeton-road, Cabbage Hall, Liverpool, a fireman on board the s.s. Trafford, swore deceased was known as the second engineer on the ressel.They reached the port of Runcorn on Saturday and tied up at the old dock. Deceased and himself came ashore on Saturday for stores, and again on the Sunday night between 7 and 8 p.m. On the Sunday night they went to the Queen's Hotel, and remained there drinking" big gills " until 10 o'clock. They then turned out with a number of other men. Witness remembered that much,and thought that be and Tucker were drunk, but subsequently his recollection left him. The next recollection ot the night's affair that witness had was that he was knocking at the lock-keepers hut Tee lock-keeper, however, would not let him go on his way until a constable was fetched, and later the con- stable took O'Hare to the doctor's and to his ship, because he complained of Isle back.—By Superintendent Pearson : He did not remember any disturbance on the canal side.

Constable John Shaw, of Runcorn, who was on duty in Waterloo-road, about 10.15 p.m. on the Sunday night testified to seeing ten me ~ all apparently sailors, stand- ing at the corner of Duke-street, near the Queen s Hotel. They were talking very loudly so he went in their direction. They evidently saw him coming for they walked frem near the Q seen's Hotel,to the entrance of the Duke Stables,and subsequently in the direction of the arches and the docks. One of them called out to the others "Look out ! Look who is following us !" He then followed the men as far as theairches but as they walk ,d straight and quieted down, he returned to his beat. About one 5.00. the following day he saw James Bolton, a constable in the employ or the Manchester Ship Canal Company, and assisted him with the last witness, O'Hare, to the doe. I tors and to his ship. O'Hare was sober and complained , of his back. Hs could not identify either deceased or O'Hare as being amongst ths men. ' John Parr lock tender, 56 Irwell-lane, said he was on duty at his hut on Sunday night. About 5 minutes past 10 p.m., a rush of about 8 or 9 men came round by his hut and began a discussion. He did not know any of them, but he should say they were a mixture of townsmen and sailors. They stood by his hut for about half an hour and kept up a quarrelsome discussion all the time They then moved about 50 or 90 yards further down the path in the direction of the Docks, and s'opped again for half an hour and engaged in a terrific discussion. " 1 hey quarrelled with their tongues, but he did not see anything of the nature of a fight.' Alter that they moved off and he did not hear any more of them. He then went to the spot where the men had been, to sea if all was right, or whether any of them had lain down there as they were all drunk. Robert Moore. Canal Constable, Hill Cottages, Higher I Runcorn, discovered the body of the dereased about 4 o'clock on the 29th tut, as the result of dragging the Chapel Basin, consequent on receiving information that a man was missing from the es Trafford. His reason for dragging that portion of the Bridgewater Canal first was because he saw a cap floating in the water when water, was being drawn off previously. The spot where the body was recovered would be immediately opposite w ere the witness Parr said the second discussion had taken place. There was also a strong two railed iron fence between the Canal and the path, and the fence would be about 4 feet high and 7 feet from the canal. Constable Carrington, Runcorn, who seseivea the body from the last witness conveyed lit to the mortuary. In his opinion there were no marks of violence upon it, and only some slight scratches on the face and back of the head. The bedy was fullit clothed and there were two halfpennies and a cl•sp knife in the pockets. The Coroner observed that the inquiry would be ad- journed for the purpose of a post eisirtos examination. A Juryman : But what it we don't fsel inclined to adjourn ? Have we a say in the matter? The Coroner : I am afraid not.

The juryman : And what if we refuse to again serve? The Coroner: You will be bouad to serve,and if yon rouil to accept the recogniz inc.- you will be handed over to His Majeity's keeping. (Luber.) The juryman : Then it is Hobson's choice. (In- creased laughter.) ThP inquiry was then adjourned to May 6th at 2.30 p.m.

div.head: CONSERVATISM IN NEWTON
div.p: CONSERVATISM IN NEWTON
DIVISION.
Colonel Pilkington, M.P., on the Budget Proposals.

The annual general meeting of the Newton Division Conservative Association was held on Sat- arday, in tho Town Hall, Newton-le-Willows, Mr C B F Borron presiding over a numerous attendance of members.

Thu Chairman, in opening the proceedings, , alluded to the loss the country had sustained in the death of Queen Victoria, and went on to say that the chief question before our minds during the past year had been the progress of the war in South Africa, and the efforts of our generals to maintain our position out there. They had seen what our generals had done, and what our Government had done, and he was sure the country was satisfied toat every effort was being made to bring the war Ito a conclusion—(hear, hear)—and to establish peace and prosperity in the country. They had to regret the great losses which had been sustained amongst those who devoted themselves to the country's cause, and that morning they had re- ceived confi-mation of the loss a member of that association had sustained in the death of his son, Sergeant Owbridge,who had died facing the enemy. The war had proved very expensive, but the Gov- ernment had handled the financial problems so as to meet the heavy demands upon the country in a way which would meet with general apprecia- tion. (Hear, bear.)

Mr W Holland Owen, the loon eecretary, then read the annual report, which alluded to the steady progrese of the assoei,,tion, and to the satisfactory organisation work which had been accomplished. The finances were also in a very sound condition,and the number of mem- bers load increased.

On the motion of Mr William Smith, seconded tiy Mr Cooper, the reports were approved. Mr W Coiling wood proposed a vote of thanks to lord Gerard, the president, and also his re-election.—Mr Richardioi seconded, and the resolution was carried with acclamation.

Colonel Richard Pilkingtov, M.P., moved a vote of thanks to the hon treasurer, the hen auditors, and the hen secretary and bon solicitors to the association. —Mr Forshaw secooded,and the resolutica was adodted. Messrs L. A. Voisey and R Barton were re-elected hors auditors. and Dr Bandysidn and Mr Barton were again appointed representatives to tbe Lancashire and Cheshire Union of Conservative Associations.

Mr W. Valiant then moved the following resolution: —"That this the annual general meeting of the Newton Division Conseraative Association earnestly desires Co congratulate Lord Salisbury and his Government upon their return to power, and looks with every confidence to a settlement of the South African question upona permanent and equitable basis calculated to ensure the lasting power of Great Britain in those regions, and we furthor desire to express our fall and unabated approval of the general -loinestic policy now being formulated by his Majesty's Ministers." He said in the recent election the country had shown by returning the Government with a very large majority that it looked upon the Con- ssrvative party as the proper persons to bring the wax to a satisfactory settlement. As to the Budget, he thought both coal and sugar were well able to bear the taxes imposed upon them. (Bear, hear.) Mr J F Smith seconded, and the resolution was sdps ported by

Colonel Pi kineton, M.P., who said, speaking gene?, ally, he, concurred thoroughly in the Budget of the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer. Flo thought Sir Mlchael &eke- Beach had in a wise, cautious and judicious manneX framed his Budget, not perliays in a sentimental ways but in a suffieietst wayto meet tee wants of the country. With regard to the duty on exporeed coal, there had been various reasons given why this Icaa a very satis- factory tax, and also why it was rot satisfactory, but there was one reason which seemed to him neither right nor statesmanlike, and that was that the coal trade having had a very good time it was now fair game fox taxation. Such a reason was unjust and flippant, and no statesman would dream ot putting it forward. But there were reasons why coal should be taxed, and the present Chancellor of the Exchequer, Sir Robert Peel. and Mr Gladstone had all agreed that coal was one of of our greatest assets, and when it was gone the prosperity of England would very likely go with it. The man in the street argued that our manufactures depended almost entirely on the coal supply, and also the comfort and happinesse of on, , homes, and, that being so, he did not like to see this coal going out of the country and being used by foreign countries we had no coal to make all sorts of things with which they actually undersold LI3 ia our own markets. The same idea referred to our n.ivy. In South Wales he believed, there was the finest eteam coal in the world, and why, he asked, shoutd foreign navies get the benefit of this coal and not pay something to the Imperial Exchequer of the United Kingdom for the privilege of using it ? When they CaLllB to look at the question in that light it was perfectly justifiable that a tax should be placed on the coal that ge.es out of the country, and he hoped the Chancellor of the Exchequer would stead to his guns in this matter. As to the sugar dutv,he was very pleased with that. Immense quantities of bounty-fed sugar bad been poured into this country from the Continent, and everybody had been wondering for several years at the cheapne,s of sugar ; and tie conaklered,now that a duty was placed upon it, it was a perfectly and absolutely satisfactory tax, and justifiable. with the duty the price would now be about 16. SI per cwr, as against 33a 9d in 1887 so this pro- duct was well able to bear duty, and especially when they remembered that almost the entire consumption of the country was bounty-fed sugar. (Rear, hear.) Be held, as a matter of principle, that the Imperial Governs merit was entitled to take at ones every farthing of the b )utey that the foreign country had put on—(bear,bear.) —and he wondered that was no', acknowledged by botn sides in Parliament as a sound and just principle. The Liberals said they wend have nothing to do with such a doctrine, as it was against free trade, arid on the Con- servative side somehow or other they were afraid of it, but to his mind it was not against free trade,and be felt that any beauty given to the foreign producer ought to go into the pocket of our Government to defray the national expenditure of tbe country. With regard to the income-tax, he knew it was a war tax, and as such it seemed reasonable and fair that twopence should be put on, and they should be satisfied that the increase was so reasonable. As to the loan of sixty millions, the country would not feel it to any great extent. Much had been said about the cost of the war, but when people spoke about the limits of taxation they were talking nonsense. They could leek back with satisfaction to the fact that the Unionist Government had been able to retrieve the disastrous policy of Sir Gladstone in 1881 and 1884. and to remove a stain frorc British starerm instill) and the British Army. (Apdlauss.) The resolution was adopted. The Chairman then proposed a v•ite of thaeke to Colonel Pilkington for his services in Paritament, and ennerniulatine him on his unopposed return to the House of Commons, and assuring him of their con- tinued and unabated support in the future. Mr Mathers secondecLand the resolution was cordially approved. The proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the chairman for presiding.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
MINOR GASES.
Warrington Borough Court.

FRlDAY—Before the Mnyor (in the chair) Councillors Smet- hurst and J. Roberts and Messrs Hepherd and Thornton. THE FULNESS CABE AGAIN —Josiah Furness Great Sankey was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon Um to contribute to the maintenance of his grand-children Harold and Arthur Furness who were charge- able to the Wanington Union.—lnr Riley, of St. Helens. represented the defendant.—Mr B. Shearer atated that Harry Furness, the son of the defendant had been married three or four years, and bad two children. Some time ago the magis- trates granted a separation order upon the soa but be had not paid the amount ordered (El per week). Cot sequently the wife had tO apply to the Guardians for relief to maintain the children and I.os per week was granted. Mr Josiah Farness was asked to contribute and made an arrangement through a local solicitor, which however, was not carried out The son was sent to prison , and consequently relief was continued to the children. Thel Guardians asked for an order upon the grandfather for Us a week —An adjourned case ia which Harry Bolton Furness applied for the reduction of the maintenance order made against him was then gone into.—Furness stated that he was earning only 18s per week and ofhred to contribute Bs. Eventually the magistrates made an order for 61 per week upon Josiah Farness and 10s per week upon II B Furness. 1 CaRBOIRTVRED LoDGMCi MolMEs.—James Fielding and Hannah Healey. of Welch's-yard, were each fined 3s for keep- Ins unregistered lodging hewer: Simla Ward. also of Welci.'s-yard. whose house was described by the Chief Con- stable as a disgrace to civilization, was tined Us for a simllir offence. WAWBINS Vits: FOOTBALL MATCH. -MiChael Babbitt. 9. Albert-street , was summoned for trespassing on the London and Borth Western Railway, thereby exposing himself to risk of danger.— Detective Howells stated that defendant trespassed on the line on Good Friday for the purpose of watching the football match.—He was fined le.—Samuel Smith. 54, Cumberland-street, was fined 8s 6d.—Andrew Clancy. 3. Byes-yard 2s 6d. and George Crotsie, 13, Priory- street 5s for similar tflences. MOND-Alt.—Before Mr F Monks (in the chair), Alderman Beaton, Councillor Smethurst,and Messrs 111rchall,Wright, and Thornton. A. Toys'. U. FENCE.— Mary Newton. 4, JOlley's-court„ was summoned for using obscene language in Brick-street on Sunday. She said her daughter was deaf and dumb,and she was shouting to her what her husband had said about her.— • be of Ss and costs was imposed. TATING TO INYLUENCE THE MAGISTRATIM• Robert and Hannah WWI fi-Id. 14, Thelwall.lane. were summoned for committing a breach of the peace by being disorderly on Saturdsy night week.--Mrs Whitfield slid not appear and a warrant wise issued for her arrest.—Sergeant Smith said he saw the man kicking at the door of his house. He after- ward- picked up a stone and smashed the dour in. His wife then came up, and he used very obscene language. They want through the house and into the buck yard, from whore they could be hoard SO yards away using bad Isnguage.—The Chief Constable said the defendant hadbeen round to several magistrates and endeavoured. though of course. In vain, to influence their minds in the case. He eonsioered the pr..ctice a most objectionable one. One or two magistrates had complained to him about defendant's conduct.—Defend- ant was bound over to keep the peace, and ordered to pay the costs 3s. - - - - - -

TUESDAY—Before Mr Birchen (in the chair) Aldermen Shaw Green. and Hutchinson. and Dr Fox. DoMESTIC INFKLICITY.—Thomas Rutter WAS charged with assaulting his wife tilizabeth Rutter on Sundiy.—Complain- ant stated that on Sunday afternoon her husband came home under the influence of drink and went to aleep. When be awoli e he commenced to quarrel with her and poked his fin- gers in her eye. She remonstrated with him and he gave her a "clout." She then threw a cup et him and he kicked her on the shins and turned her out of the house.—Tide Chief Constable stated that there was a case pending against the prisoner for assaulting hie wife. He was before the magis- trates on March 29th and the case was adjourned for eight weeks In order to al:, him a chance of ref,r siing Prisoner was a well known thief.—The Bench committed prisoner to , gaol for a month and granted his wife a separation order with ' 95 per week alimony. TINZ BOY AND THF. AUTOMATIC MACHINE.—A small boy named John Moran. aged seven, was charged with wander- ing about without being under proper control.—P.G. Stuart Said that the previous morning he received a communication from the railway authorities that an automatic machine at Arpley station had been broken and pilC-red. At 930 he apprehended the prisoner who was loitering about Bank Quay Station. He questioned him as to the automatic machine and he staton that he put a penny in the slot and obtained a pi, cc of toffy. He then put in two halfpennies but the machine would not operate. Thereupon he got some stones and smashed the machine and took some toffy and some Other lads came up and stole the remainder. tle ad- mitted sleeping out three nights last week. —The Chief Con- stable applied for a remand until Friday as on that day tie boy's mother would be prosecuted for neglecting him. The boy WAS like a young avage and bit and tore at the polis- a !ikz a monkey. —Prisoner was remanded accordingly.

WLDNESDAT.—Before Messrs John White (in the chair), Joihua Ball 'Dim Armitve and J. .1. Sleekly. MIiCFLLANEoVS.--Samnel Plinston and John Brian were each fined 2s 6,1 for failing to carry lighted lamps on their -vehicles on the nights of the 25th and 26th April respectively. —George Caldwell, who did not appear, and had previously been before the magistratecwas fined 10s and costs for a simi- lar offence Woolston on April 19th.—Bernard Lmg and Willttm !details, were Aned 2s 6d and costs for drunkenness at Croft.—A. Ana of 5s and costs wa.. Imposed upon Michael Loitus for being drunk and disorderly at Newton on the previous day.—Peter Johnson, farmer, of Croft. was summoned for having in his 'possession for trade purpmes a pair of unjust scales, sod was, on the evidence of inspector Shepherd flied Its—Aaron Clarke, Woolstun, who did not appear, was fined Ifs and costs for having an nujAst 56 lb weight in his possession for use of tr .de.

div.head: Daresbury Petty Sessions.
div.p: Daresbury Petty Sessions.

ItiESDIV.—Bef ore Messrs William Long (in the chair),Joseph 1 Knowles, H Nield and Roger sAsaritoa Parr. I ALLEGIANCE TO TUE KING. —Messrs NI, id. Knowles and 1 Parr took the oath of allegian e to the King. 1 A. PoACTItIi SMARTLY DEALT WITH.---DICASE AT HILL CLiTTF..—James Hlgham was summsned for having on the 1 7th April, at Appleton, trespassed in the day-time on land in the Occupation of John Derbyshire in search of game.—Mr A Is White prosecuted.—The defendant pleaded uot. guilty.—Mr White said the facts were unusually simple or a case of this lend. On the day in question, the defendant and another man were seen by John Broady, gamekeeper, to get over a hurdle fence into a pasture field In the occupation of John Derbyshire at Hill Cliffe. The g mekeeper, who was secreted at the tiro,, observed that there was a hare in the field. The man opened out a net and proceeded to draw it across the field,when the gamekeepersaw two hares run.neither of which 'Sas caught. The two men joined company, and the defend- ant concealed the net between his waistcoat and his shirt. The game keeper came forward and the two men commenced to run. The gamekeeper called to his son, who was alto secreted, and the latter gave chase and succeeded in catching the defendant. The Other man got away. He (Mr White) contended that it was not necessary for a zonvict on that the defendant should have been found Runic of taking game ; It was sufficient for it to be proved that he was trespassing, and that there was a reasonable presnnsptlon that he was mere to take games 'lbis was the worst form of poaching It was hot a cast of sport, legitimate or illegitimate but purely. -ii commercial matter—an attempt to wrongfully take someone else's property for the purpose of making money.— Hvidence in support of the above atatement having been given, the defendant plead° 1 that he was not guilty, Re had, he said, given up poaching long ago —Superintendent Peerson said there were 12 previous Convictions against the defendant, one being for a game trespass.—Finect alla and out, the advocate's fee to be allowed. A WOMAIS'a VIEIPT.—Hgary Fut E.—/ill.abetla Ridgway, a I respectably dressed woman, wee charged with having on the 213 t Orli Stolen two fowls, of the value of Os the property a i

Albert Percival. farmer, Antrobus.—The complainant, on a 1 moonlight night was looking through a bedroom win tow when he saw Mrs Percival running away from the fowl- house. There was a man with her but be could not Identify hirn. Near the fowl house was a wire clothes lice. 41t or bit high, which knocked off Mrs Bidgeway's hat which be after- wards found on the spot. On the 29th April. the defendant (accompanied by her daughter) visited complainant at his house and said that " Joseph " bad told her that she must give him (complainant) a sovereign. A witness stated that he met the defendant on the night in question and she had no hat on her bead.—lt was proved that two fowls were missing from the hen cote.—Defendant pleaded guilty and said there was no man with her on the night of the robbery. —ln answer to the Bench, she said she did not know what induced her to go to the hen cote. She was not in want of food at home.—The defendant, who appeared to feel her position very aeutely,was fined £2 and costs, the Chairman remarkisig that the case was a very serious on. The Bench were sorry to see the de!endant in such a position. There appeared to be no excuse for the crime.

The defendant Povey,set his d,g,which was almost a thorough- bred greyhound, after a couple of hares, bet though the dog ran both, the hares e3C sped into the wood Defendants, on being accosted by Rigby, stopped and gave their nans.s. Prisoner said he was going to his flat " John Clarke' Captain Smith —" Well" said Gregory "Seeing you behave so suspiciously I will go with you—Prisoner then said "It was no use, it was all lies."—Sergeant Pearson stated that the prisoner had been under observation for the last three weeks. div.head: KAISER'S AVENUE OF STATUES.
div.p: THE KAISER'S AVENUE OF STATUES.

'There are few visitors to Berlin," says a writer in the May number of the 4* Windser Magazine,' " who have not wandered with pleasure through the beauti- ful park known as the Thierearten, which is the biggest playground of the Berliners. And now the Thier- garthn, with its wealth of statues and memorials, is re- ceiving an added attraction such as probably no such park in the whole world can boast- It already has cele- brated avenues in plenty,one oi the mostpopular for some ' years past has been the Sieges-Alice. The Kaiser has resolved i.bat there shall be erected on both sides of the Sieges-Illee statues of all the rulers of past and present times of the kingdoms of Brandenburg and Prussia. These statues are to be as artistic and:finished as pea- Bible. They are to be of the purest white marble that can be got for the purpose, and are to be modelled by , the finest sculptors that the Fatherland can produce. 1 The Kaiser has set aside over one hundred thousaed pounds for the scheme out of his °Jen private pArse, and it is his intention, when the work is completed, to hand it over as a present to the municipality for ever. There are to be thirty-two cf these statues, sixteen on either side of the avenue. Th 3 name of the famous parade, Sieges-Alice, means' The Avenue of Victory'; conse- quently it will be most appropriate that these marble memorials commemorate some of the chief victors among the monarchs and warriors of the Fatherland. Two statues will be erected to represent each period of the rule of the Elohenz)llerns. The Kaiser is responsiblef for the general style of the memorials and their design. Everything is to be carried out on a most elaborate scale. In the Centre of each group there will be a large white marble statue of the King or Elector it represents, while on each side will be the smaller statues of the two most important statesmen of that monarch's reign. These may be either Ministers of the Crown or warriors, SO long as they have contributed to the elory of the period in question. Thus such men as Bismarck and Moltke are good examples of the leseer names that will be associated with the Royal ones. bo great is the Kaiser interest in this work that he has paid meny visits to the sculptors during the progress of the several statues under their charge. tie himself went thoroughly into the matter at the outset as to which of the sculp- tors of the frattlerland were most capable of giving fitt- ing expressionta his ideas; and after much deliberation he decided who should be engaged, and the w-..,rk to be allotted to each. By thus distributing the ' 'work the Sovereign saw that not only would the greet task be completed sooner. but iffntdtheartentt ct herse ewpte,nrisd atotsoexbceelmeuacchh rivalry amongst h other's work in the eyes of their King and his people, that be would necessarily get from. them the very best work that German sculpture of the age could produce. The Kaiser wise!? resolved, too that all the work should be done by native artists, as he considered that such a national memorial should owe nothing to outside aid." ,

div.head: Batley Winners for the Third Time.
div.p: Batley Winners for the Third Time.

Warrington lost the Northern Union Challenge Cup on Saturday, being beaten in the final by Batley, who thus secured the trophy for the third time in five years. The margin in their favour was one of two tries to nil, Comments by " Ovalist " on the defeat of the local team will be found in another column. The Warrington team I left for Manchester at 9.55 and had dinner in the city, , taking train for Leeds at 11-50 and reaching their dew- ' nation in good time. Their supporters were not al for- Waste, and the special trains, to the number of ten, which left the Central and Arpley Stations, did not all I reach Leeds in time for the match. About 5.000 people left Warrington to lend their support to the " wire- pullers," but not half of them were on the ground in time to see the kick-eff. Some even did not arrive till after half-time, and a vast deal of ' disappointment was caused. Trough there were showers in the morning the weather cleared up and was all that could be desired in the afternoon. The ground at fleadiagley was in perfect condition, and there was every prospect of a fast, open game prior to the match. People rolled up in thousands in every kind of vehicle, and the attendance finally smashed all records for the Northern Union. It was estimated that there were 33,000 people present, and the receipts totalled £1,650. Warrington had a good reception on entering the enclos- ure, but the roar of applause which went up when Batley appeared showed that they were the favourites in the estimation of the bulk of the crowd. Mr J Kidd, of Millom, was the referee, and the touch judges Mr J Oak- land (Oattwood Church) ; and Mr J Bruckshaw (Stockport). Warriogton won the toss, and Isherwood gave Batley the advantage of playing with the wind behind them, but with the sun in their faces. Oakland kicked off fire minutes late, and Dickenson returned to Fezgerald, who punted. Batley were, however, called back for off-side play, ard the first scrummage took place at the centre. From this Bate kicked to Garner, who missed the ball, but Stubley saved smartly. A kick by one of the Batley backs took play back to mid-field, and here more scrum- mages were fought. Midgley twice missed the ball when it came out at his side of the scrummage. Then a punt out sent the ball to Garner, who for the second time mulled badly. Davies tried to recoeter, but slipped on the line and lost the ball, Duckworth coming up and running over at the corner- The ball was, however, called back—a piece of hard luck for Warrington. The next item was a penalty-kick on the touch-line, taken by F sh. The three-quarter kicked well, but the wind carried the ball outside. Davies now ran and kicked smartly, and Hallam ran into touch in his own quarters in kicking the ball. A feature so far had been the capital fielding of the Warrinron bseks. Now, how- ever, Hallam made a mistake, He kicked badly in his own half, and Isherwood, to whom the ball was carried by the wind, missed it. A Batley forward dribbled away, but Fish came to the rescue of his side in clever fashion, and kicked out of dange?. After Scholtzo had been cautioned for charging, Davies had a penalty kick, at mid-field. He rdeeed the ball, but his shot was both low and Short, a-d Dickenson punted away, warremiee bad a penalty at. halt-way. and the ball went to D 'vies, who made a clever corkscrew run, and gained ground before being tackled. A minute later Barley scored threugh a bad piss by Isherwood to Dickenson. That player misfiled the pass, and Goodall took advantage of the mistake in very clever fashion. He picked up smartly and ran grandly down the field to the line. Davies was in close attendance, and taking his pass within five yard. of the posts leered a neat try in a favourable position amidst a scene of great enthusiasm, the Batley partisans cheering wildly. Davies took the shot at goal, but kicked up a clod of earth and the ball failed to rise. The Batley backs were kicking with great effect, and it was evident that the Warrington backs were very nervous. They missed the ball fre- quently, and another mull by Dickenson gave Batley their second try. This player first misfielded and then had his kick charred, the remit being that the game was taken to the Warrineten line. Here a scrummage was fought, and from this Oakland dodged to the line, where he was pulled desamlunder the posts- However, from the pack which followed Oakland passed to Mieg- ler, who threw to Fitzgerald. 'The last named passed to Auty, who ran in smartly at the corner. Daires made a poor attempt at goal, but with a lead of six points Batley people were on good terms with themselves. After the kick-off Isherwood improved matters for his side by a clever run and kick, which took the game into his opponents' varterst. Here Battey were penalised, and Fish tried at goal from a fairly good position, but again without result. Goodall at length kicked down the field, and Isherwood tried in vain to get les side out of difficulties. Eden charged Garner over after the tatter had kicked, and Mr. Kidd seeing the incident, penalised Warrington. Judge this time took the plaee, but the ball struck one of the uprights, and rebounded into play. To make matters worse for their side, the Warrington backs made several more mulls, and it was not until their forwards enecuted a neat dribble that their lines were cleared They got mere relief subse- quently from a long kick by Fitzgerald, the ball being allowed to go dead. Another kick by one of the Batley titmice yielded one more . minor, and then the Warrington backs executed some passing RA the result of Fitzgerald missing a trans- fer from Oakland. Isherworld snapped the ball up and passed to Dickenson. who nessed the ball. Harris wag, however, at hand, and made a little ground, but Davies ran and kicked well down the field. He was obstructed by 'slier weed, whose name was taken by the referee, while Batley were awarded a penalty kick, Devi a took the plane near the touch-line, land kicked finely hut the wind carried the ball outside. Batley continued to press hotly, And up to this point the Werrineten men had not shown the slightest evidence of the form that hed carried them through the ties. Eventually Bate burst away splendidly, and a try looked certain for either Isherwood or Fish, but the half-back's pass was takn by Auty who kicked 'town the field. The around was, however, lost through one of the Batley forwards being off-side. Fish and leherwood then tried passing, but without success, and the next item was the cautioning of Fish and Auty for fighting when on toe greund. The caution was administered on the report of Mr Oakland, one of the touch-judges. The interval was reached a minute later. with Batleg leading by six points. Half-time Score :—Batley, 2 tries (6 neints) ; Warringten, nil. Isherwood restarted, and Judge replied into touch at mit'fleld. Here Fish had a shot at goaeowing to Batley having failed to put the ball into the scrummage straight, but once more ho missed the iansanreka.oyßoavtleery. now had to defend, and scrummages were fought at their quarter-line. Here Bate got away, and passed to Elitainrrii:,awtchloatineradlreis.tli bhraidllia hoanstrt a run, and aoaLstraight with the posts, at the Batley quarter-line,but once more the shot failed, to the great disappointment of the Warrington people. A long kick yielded a minor to Warrington and delay occurred, owing to an injerr to Fitzeerald, who was sliehtly injured, and required much rubbing by his colleogivis. For some time play was at the centre, and had now we here Batley were penalised for obstraction. Fish tricked, but Goodall replied family well, and now an unpleasant lecident occurred, Maine being Sent off the field o stage n a of eroudghpelraoyu.s. Theß‘tl b ey tatd only 14 men, but they looked like scoring again, Fitz- gerald passing to Davies, who Was, however, held tor Harrie when be locked anz brought down the field by the dribbling of teas Warring- ton forwards, and the L aneasarians were nearly over. u The Batley backs relieved* little by passite, het Good- all field. dk. "Acek t Batteywhen backs p they looked sse em d like r, gi ntf p th u t Fitz- gerald 's transfer to Auty watt forward. On Batley being penalised Isherwood kicked to his opponents line, where Fitzeerald made his Mark. Then Bate ran smartly from a scrummage, but was unable to get through. Hallam next kicked a little too far, and Judge sent the ball Idead, Garner was new injured, but soon reacivered, land Batley bad a warm time on tha defence
THE EXAMINER, FR WAN, MAY 3, 1901.

until their forwards dribbled away, and Fisk made a very feeble effort to check them. The Batley people were delighted when Auty tacklei Fish cleverly, but Warrington were now almost con tinually on the attack, and Bate and Duckworth made a big effort to get over, which, however, was unsuc- cessful. Then came a brilliant bit of play on the part of Davies. He got the ball in his own quarters, and ran finely up the field. When be reached Hallam he kicked, and beating the full back and Dickenson,almost recovered possession on the Warrington line. Dickenson was just successful in getting the ball,but Davies tackled him, and he passed to !Tanana, who was also tackled by the little Batley three-quarter, amid cheering. War- rington were penalised in their quarters, and Davies had a shot at goal from near the touch line. Be kicked well ' but the ball went outside. The Warrington forwards got away down the field after this, and Bate following up a kick, nearly nor ed, Davies just coming up in time and kicking dead. Batley once more took up the runn- ing, and Warrington bad to defend. From a scrum- mage at the Warriegton " 25" Oakland got away, and passed to Fitzgerald, who ran over near the posts,only to be called back for a throw forward. Still, Batley pressed hotly, until they were penalised for off-aide play at the scrummage. Their kick did them Ino good, for their forwards were in front at the punt, and scrummages took place near the Warrington posts. Warrington were given another ' penalty kick for an informality at the scrummage, and the ball was kicked to Davies, who punted over the line, scoring • minor point. Eventually the Lancas- trians reached the centre, and Garner missed the ball from a kick. Hanle followed up well, but was unable to get possession, and a good opening was lost. Flay was warmly contested at midfield, and another delay occurred owing to Harris being so badly hurt that he had to be carried off the field. The best bit of passing the match bad produced now took place, the ball going through the h mds of the half backs, Isherwood, Dickenson and Fish. The last-named ran brilliantly al- most to the line, but was unable to get throaela, and Batley tbus won a poor match by the half-time score. ' Result •-13atley, 2 tries, 6 points ; Warrington, nil. Thir defeat on Saturday made Warrington all the more determined to win the South-West Lancashire Cup, which was played for at Wigan on Monday evening. The advantage was all Leigh way, for their men had been saving themselves for the match, while Warrington euffered consicierably as a result of the contest with Bat ey. No less than five of the regular players were unavailatle, the absentees being Bate and Duckworth (halve;), Harris (threecriarter), Scholtze and Cunning- ' ham (forwards). There was plenty of interest in the encounter in Warrington, and the team was followed by Close urine a thousand spectators, who thronged the 4.501 and 5.20 trains to Wigan. Leigh were only poorly sup- ported. Rain had fallen slightly during almost the wholel of the day, but the ground was in excellent order, though the arrangements made by the Wigan club were very inadequate. The stand was 'rushed," and a great' many peopie got into the enclosure without paying any- thing. As time wrnt on the crowd increased.in dimen- sions, and there would be fully 8,000 spectators present ' before the close of the match. div.head: LIBERAL SECRETARIES AND AGENTS. – Lancashire and Cheshire Branch.
div.p: LIBERAL SECRETARIES AND AGENTS. - Lancashire and Cheshire Branch.

The annual meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire branch of the National Association of Liberal Secretaries and Agents was held on Monday at the Liberal Club, Bleckpool, Mr H B Shores in the chair. Forty-five agents were present. The report of the Executive Com- mittee was adopted. The treasurer presented his state- ment, which showed a substantial credit balance. The honorary officers—Mr El B Shores (Widnes), chairman ; Mr C A Walls, treasurer ; and Mr S Schofield, hon. secretary—were reappointed. Messrs Walls (North Salford), Harrison (Dirwen), Wi;ler (Noitti-Ese, Man- chester), Whitehead (Oldham), Birtwistle (Accrington), and Barlow (ttamabottom), were appointed to represent the branch, upon the Central Council. Messrs Handley (Runcorn), Gerry (Bolton), and Durham (Southport) were elected members, of the Executive Committee. The Chairman produeed and explained the draft ruled for the proposed new Society of Liberal agents, which would take effect upon the amalgamation of the two existing societies. The agents were enter- tained by Mr James Hodgson, president of the Black- pool Liberal Association. After the toast of " The King." that of" Our Host" was proposed by Mr A Mins, and responded to by Mr Hodgson. "The Liberal Agents," was proposed by Councillor Wilde, and re- sponded to by Mr LI B Shores. "The Town and Trade of Blackpool" was proposed by Mr Whiteheal, and responded to by Mr Thomas Gent. " Our Local Agent, Mr Home,' was proposed by Mr Sam Schofield,to which Mr Herne replied.

div.head: N.S.P.C.C.
div.p: THE N.S.P.C.C.
Annual Meeting of the Warrington Branch.

Address by the Rev. B. Waugh. The Mayor (Alderman Roberts) presided over tie annual meeting of the Warrington branch of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, which was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall on Thursday last week. There was a large attendance of ladies and those inter- ested in the work of this worthy society. . . .

The CHAIRMAN said he did not think it was necessary for him to say anything to coltnmend the society to the people of Warrington, but he thought he should only be saying what was true if he said that perhaps the want of intimate personal knowled;e of the , society's operations which unfortunately characterized ' a great many of them, had to some extent accounted for the fact that the local subscription list, upon which of course, everything to a large exteet depended, had not been as comprehensive or as large in amount as the objects of the society demanded and freely justified. He hoped the result of the meeting that day, and the inter- eating facts which were contained in the annual report—many of which be could personally vouch for their accuracy—would tend to increase the interest which a Society of this kind so fully deserved. He also hoped that Warrington instead of being as it was at the present time—to some extent perhaps owing to the separation of the Warrington districts from Altrincham —dependent upon the national fund for part of the re- sources necessary to carry on its work. would be self- supporting, and that instead of needing assistance from outside, would in course of time, not only pay for the operations conducted within its own borders, but might do some little to asaist the funds of those districts which were not self-supporting because of the compara- tive poverty of the people living in tnem. (Applause.)
THE ANNUAL REPORT.

The annual revirc ut the work done in the War- rington district was submitted. It read as fellows :—ln presenting their report for the year ending March 31st, 1901, your committee wish to urge in the strongest way possible the claims Of the society to more generous sut, port, and the need of an organized band of workers to make known throughout the district the substantial work which is being done. During the year Mr W B Greener, who served the society for nine years as honor. ary secretary, retired from the office, in consequence of his removal to Wakefield, and your committee wish to place on record their very high appreciation of his ser- vices, invulving almost daily conterences with the inspector during that period, and the conflict with special difficulties which beset the society in the estab- lisbment of this branch. Owing to the absence during the last year or two of Mrs Greenell, the late treasurer, and prior to the election of Mrs Aylmer Frost as her successor, the organization of the branch has suffered, and your committee hope that during the coming year ladies' committees will be re-formed in various parts of the district. The appointment of an Inspector for the Altrincham district and the formation of a sioarate branch there, including Lymrn, caused thelose to this district of sub- ' scriptions amounting to £207 14s lid per annum, and though this alteration withdrew a considerable area and r. large poputation from the district worked by this branch, the number of cases actuilly dealt with has been greater than in any previous year, only 11 cases out of 400 being dropped on investigation, making 389 actu- ally dealt with ; whereas 27 cases the year before were dropped eut of 409, leaving 382 cases dealt with. The 400 cases investigated affected the welfare of 1,401 chil- dren-683 boys and 718 girls. The prosecutions during the year amounted to 38, and the sentences of imprison- ment in the aggregate to 9 yeare and 6 months. 1.025 supervision visits were made by the Inspector. Your Committee wish to impress upon their supporters the very great usefulness of this branch of the work. The result of it has been that hundreds of homes in the dis- trict have been cleansed, and the condition of the chil- dren greatly, improved during is year ; but the num- ber of cases to be dealt with s far too large for one Inspector, and the Director of the Society (Rev 13 Waugh) has expressed a wish to appoint another Inspec- tor to take up oases in Runcorn, Widnes, and Frodsham. Your Committee agree that this ouget to be done, but their financial prospects at present do not justify the additional expense, at d they therefore appeal to their supporters to help them in extending the work. In fulfilment of his duty he Inspector has received much help from the School 'Attendance Officers, which your Committee gratefully acknowledge ; it is also with no less satisfaction that they place on record the very valuable aid of the Chief Constable and his staff, who have shown a real appreciation of the work of the Society, and to whom many thanks are due. Daring the year the Inspector has visited many of the Elemen- tary Schools in the district, and would acknowledge, through your committee, the unfailing courtesy with which he has been received by the schoolmasters and mistresses. It is also with very great satisfaction that your cemmittee can review the conscientious and pains. taking work of Inmector Hackett during the past twelve months, and can heartily congratulate him on baying won the respect and confidence of all who have had dealings with him. May he ever receive the gratification which is due to such faithful service.

Local Case in the Chancery Court. Before Vice-Chancellor Hall at the Lancashire Chancery Court on Monday the case of Monks v Tysons, from Warrington, which had reference to the administration of the estate of Samuel Horrocks, who died in 1883 was heard. The estate consisted of mortgages principally, the total being about £7,700 Three trustees were originally appointed,but in 1896, the survivor, Mr Tysons died and his widow hecpe hie legal reprbsentadve. Mr Widdowsou,solicitor,then consented to be appointed trustee, and he was appointed by deed on Septem- ber 9, 1896. Mr Monks was also appointed a trustee Subsequently Mr Widdowson presented a bill for services rendered amounting to £5O, of which £8 58 was for costs out of pocket. Mr J Rutherfori, on behalf of the co-trustee, Mr Monks, argued that Air Widdowson, was not entitled to remuneration for the work in question, which was done either after his formal appointment as trustee, or shortly before, and within the time in which he consented to be a trustee,many of the charges relating to the negotia- tions for the appointment of the new trustees.—Mr C Wilson, on behalf of the beneliciares, supported .1 he contention of Mr Butherford,—Mr Maberly. for the defence, submitted that there was no authority to show that a solicitor prior to his actual appointment as trustee was not entitled to remuneration for services rendered.—The Vice- ChanPellor said his chief difficulty was at what date :Mr Widdowson became de fa:to a trustee. There could be no question as to his right before he agreed to become a trustee,but the question of costs oetween that date and the formal deed of accept- ance was open to argument. The matter had better stand over for evidence on that point, arid for authorities, if they could be found, on the point. There would also be liberty to cross-examine Mr Widdowson if so desired. The case was then adjourned.
