div.head: BRAVERY REWARDED.
div.p: BRAVERY REWARDED.

A Warrington Girl Receives a Humane Society's Medal. Interesting Presentation. There was an interesting ceremony at the War- rington Police Court en Friday morning when Miss Florence Ratcliffe, a girl of about 18, who resides at 13, Tanners'-lane was the recipient of a silver medal and a framed certificate from the Liverpool Shipwreck and humane Society. The magistrates on the Bench were the Mayor (presiding), Coun- cillors Smethurst and J Roberts and Messrs Thorn- ton and Hepherd.

The Mayor said that before they opened the court he bad an extremely pleasing duty to per- form. It wam in consequence ot a letter which he received two days ago from the Liverpool Ship- wreck and Humane Society, asking him if he would on their behalf present to Miss Florence Ratcliffe a silver medal and vote of thanks awarded by the Society to her for conspicuous gallantry in rPscuing three children from a house which was on tire on January 18th. He was quite sure that an occasion of that kind was one which fortunately or unfortu- nately, which ever way they liked to take it, did not occur too often, but it was an extremely pleasant thing for him to have the opportunity of publicly recognizing, not only on behalf of the Society, but on behalf of the town, the brave conduct of Mies Ratcliffe. His Worship then narrated the circum- stances of the occer..,ece, from which it appeared that Miss Ratcliffe wl.s going to her work on Friday afternoon, January 18th, and when passing a house in Orford-street, noticed a considerable amount of smoke issuing through the front door. She also heard the cries of children. She entered the house, and was unable to see owing to the density of the smoke. She brought out one child, then returned and brought the other two. Continuing, the Mayor said that an occasion of this kind was not only most agreeable to reflect upon, but did infinite credit to the person capable of such heroism He should not be doing his duty if he did not ex- press his extreme gratification that they bad among them a girl of such pluck and bravery, and he was sure that as long as Miss Ratcliffe lived— and he hoped she might have a long and useful life before her—this circumstance would always afford her great satisfaction and she would feel that at any rate she had done some s3rvice to her fellows, 'worth3 of being remembered as long as she lived. Miss Ratcliffe was then conducted on the Bench and the Mayor pinned the medal on her breast, impressing the hope that she would live for many years in health and strength to wear it. In handing her the certificate he said he hoped it would remind her and all with whom she was con- nected of the act of bravery which was very credit- able to her. (Applause.)
Cheshire. Lines Workmen's Provident Society.

The 26th annual meeting of the Cheshire Lines platelayers' and Workmen's Provident Society, which consists of the workmen employed in the Engineer's Department of the Cheshire Lines Rail- way,' was held at the Works, Battersby-lane, War- rington, on Tuesday. In the unavoidable absence of the Chief Engineer, Mr W G Scott, C E, the chair was taken by Mr F Fowden, and the meeting was largely attended by officials and delegates from Lancashire and Cheshire. The Secretary submitted the annual report, which stated that the number of members was 1,163. A large SUM bad been expend- ed in aid of 284 sick members, who had received assistance from the funds of the Society, and 31 death claims had also been paid. The report and statement of accounts having been passed, Mr Thomas Pratt was re-elected secretary for the en- suing year, and Messrs George Walker and Robert Jones were re-elected Auditors.

div.head: Lettcrs to tbe Obator. Sunday Concerts and a Great Crime.
div.p: Lettcrs to tbe Obator. Sunday Concerts and a Great Crime.

Sir—l have been interested in the correspondence relating to the holding of sacred concerts on Sundays. I have absolutely no empathy with merely Sabbatarian objections to a pleasant Sunday afternoon or evening of this nature, and few people are now impressed with the heinousness of whistling on the " Sabbath." I believe in making Sunday a respectful and recuperative institution in every sense. It is difficult to conceive of any valid objection to sacred concerts as such, and I should be rather inclined to support some such form of Sunday recreation,if managed under the supervision,say of the Corporation, with an educational object and not for "private profit, gain, or by way of trade." I may not be thoroughly acquainted with the merits of the case under discussion, bat it seems to me that the Free Churches are altogether too modest in the scop3 of their aggressive operations. I think they might have shot at nobler Ramo. For nearly two years the town has been bruttliz -id by the war fever. A crime of un- paralleled magnitude, in modern times has been corn- , mitted, and my opinion is th tr, this might have been ended months ago,many valuable lives have been saved, and a nation's fair name retrieved, if the Free Churches had used their power to that end. I have longed to bear some strong voice in Warrington speak against the rampant Hooligans of war during the past eighteen months, and the silent attitude of the churches has been most painful to bear. Imagine then my irritation, while waiting for this voice when I dis- covered that the Church artillery was being brought into position to prevent concerts obtaining a footing in the town ! I have no desire to say one dis- respectful word against those who have protested against this assumed desecration cf the Sabbath but it does seem that sad) a proceeding, in view of the silent connivance of the churches in a great crime, bears a ndlcrous resemblance to breaking a fly on the wheel,— Y ,urs szc., THOMAS EDMONDSON.

Infirmary Subscriptions. Sir,-1 beg to draw the attentionlot the public, and ;working men generally, to:the very inadequate amount 0 subscriptions coming in to support the Infirmary, and as the above Institution is so indispensable to all the Working Classes and supported by voluntary sub- scriptions, renewed efforts are absolutely necessary. I implore one, and all, to make increased eff _ins to carry en the noble work, of helping those who cannot help themselves, through accident or otherwise. Some people would think it almost incredible,that the cases relieved at the Dispensary for the past twelve months, amount to the astounding numsier of 5979, a fact we should not loge sight of. We must also consider the number of cases where patients are treated at their own homes. The Infirmary being full, and the increas- ing population of Warrington, will involve the addition of another wing to the Infirmary.in the very near future. The Warrington and District Nursing Association is another noble institution, where the nurses are ever ready, like ministering angels, to render kindly help, and have already given comfort to many sad homes,and soothed many a sick and dying pillow. To allow this Institution to lapse, would be a calamity second only to the less of the Infirmary. I beg to suggest, that the employees of all the firms in town and district, of whatever branch of trade, should contribute one halfpenny per week,—a merely nominal sum, and within the reach of all classes. This would realize a very handsome total, the collection of which could be arranged with their employers. I would that some pen more able than mine, could have taken this important matter up, and dealt with the procedure in a more lucid and concise form, than this, my poor effort—l be to remain. Sir, Yours respectfully, JOHN RIGBY.

"Mercury," and the Trades Council. Sir,—l am sorry to trouble you further but really the wilful misrepresentation of my statements deliberately made by your correspondent, J," calls for a reply. I have not " trounced the Trades Council for forwarding labour representation," but because it attempted to in- troduce by a side issue the question of Trades Unionism into a contest where there was not a simple shred of justification for it on any question of principle affectiug either the interests of Trades Unionism or Labour. I have not said that "Accountants " are the only men qualified for the position of elective auditors, but that only such men as are well versed in figures and genorally accustomed to deal with accounts are eqiial to the re- sponsibilites of such a position. lam not goiter to apologise for stating as a fact that quite a large proportion of the 193111n9 of the indivi- duals who have been reported as speaking at the meetings of Trades Council are those of well-known Insurance agents, nor for calling attention to the further fact that practically all the " Labour" candidates at the recent election of Guardians, were Insurance agents and stated that they were "supported by the Trades Council." if" P.J." would only be more caretul in his reading of my letters and allow his mind to really grasp what I hare said before rushing into print and attribut- ing statements to me which I have never made, he would be a much more agreeable and worthy op- ponent. In regard to Mr Stott, I am sure I am grateful to him for bic " compliment " but I fear I cannot appreciate it as he intends because I am not conscious that I at any tim in this controversy have said anything intended to be personally effensive. My opponetrs on the contrary, in each case in their first replies indulged in " picturesque" language concerning my poor self with a freedom which lacked either wisdom or justification. lam really glad, there- fore, that in this second and "final "letter Mr Stott has mproved so vastly upon his first attempt. I must,how- ever, correct one or two rather serious errors into which Mr Stott has fallen. I have not indulged in " cheap sneers" at the result of the election in BewsevlWard and lam not " delighted " with the result. If I had been a voter there Mr Plinston would have had my

support, but I think his defeat in a thoroughly working class ward fully justifies my contention that to put forward " Insuranco agents "as labour candidates is such an obvious anomaly that the result is a foregone eonalusion. With the greater portion of Mr Stott's letter lam in entire sympathy. lam a Trades Unionist in principle, and have always been so, hut I cannot and do not approve of thri forced introduction of Trades Unionism into matters with which it has no concern. and the effect of which illegitimate intrusion is only to bring discredit. As to Mr Flanagan—well I am sorry that he has made such an exhibition of himself in his last letter. One thing is quite certain and that is that he is not over- burdened with modesty, neither is it necessary for him to ask the Lord to •• gie him a guid conceit o' hissel." lam sure your readers will gratefully appreciate Mr Flanagan's kindness in potting aside for their benefit his deep seated objection to anything which might have the appearance of " Self glorification " in revealing to them the wonderf al list of qualifications which he claims to possess, and which by this time certainly ought to have landed him high up the ladder of fame. ' At last he has ceased to "bide his light under a bushel " and has most veritably set it on a "candlestick." One thing I may say without fear of contradiction mod that is that Mr Flanagan has not taken the " gruel" which be gives me credit for having administered to him either like a " man or an Englishman," but I will not imitate the gross vulgarity into which he has descended by suggesting that his attitude in this respect is that of " an unmitigated cad."—Yours, MERCURY. Correspondence on this subject must now cease—RD. "Examiner."

div.head: Fate of Sergeant Owbridge.
div.p: The Fate of Sergeant Owbridge.

Information was received at Earlestown on Saturday afternoon which definitely sets at reEt the doubt, res- pecting the fate of Sergeant A Owbridge, of .the 32nd Company Imperial Yeomanry.—lt will perhaps be remembered that a fight occurred at Z ekoe River, in which the 32nd Company of Imperial Yeomanry, under the command of Captain Bretherton, was engaged. In the list of casualties it was stated that 8973, Sergeant A Stowbridge, 32nd Company Imperial Yeomanry was killed. Many people at once came to the coclusion that this was a mistake, and that it referred to Sergeaut A Owbridge, of Wargrave-road, Earlestown. His wife and parents, however, held to the hope that it was not him, and enquiries were set on font for the purpose of clear- ing up the mystery, Lord Newton considerably inter ested himself, and after the lapse of three weeks. Mrs Owbridge reepived a telegram from the War Office, stating that 8974, Sergeant A Owbridge was killed April 6th at Zeekoe River. The sad news spread like wildfire through the town, and there were many expressions of sympathy with the family, not alone from the towns, people, but from Lord N.. Jean, Lord Gerrard, Colonel Pilking,tcn, M P.. and others, and the flag at the Con- servative Club wag hoisted half-mist. Mr Robert Stone. J.P.' of Newton Park, showed his kindly feeling by per- sonally callicg upon the family on Tuesday night, and expressing his deep sympathy with them in thee affir- tion.

On Sunday evening, at Wargrave Church, after the service, Mr E Leyland, the organist, played the Dead March, Mr 0 wbridge having been a sideman at the I church. On Sunday morning neat, a memorial service will be held, when the members of the Orange Lodge of which the deceased was a member, will wade, and led by the Earlestewn band, attend the service. The Men's Bible Class connected with St John's Church, and con- ducted by Mr Thomas Molyneux, will also attend the service, prior to which they will form a square in front of the residence of Mr 0 wbridze, senior, and accom- panied by the Land will sing verses of the favourite hymn "Rock of Ages." and of the mission hymn" Old be with you." The C troop of Lancashire Hussars of which deceased was a member, will, so far as at present arranged, attend service at St Peter's Church, Newton, but efforts are being made to secure their attendance at the memorial service at Wargrave.

HOMECOMING VOLUNTEERS. Arrival of the Cheshires. The steamer Tagus, with Volunteer contingent's from South Africatarrived at Southampton on Monday morn- ing. Among those on board were officers and men of the Cameron Highlanders, Royal West Kent Regiment, Duke of Cornwall's Light Infantry,Gordon Highlanders, Border Regiment. Wiltshire Regiment, let London En- gineers,Seaforth Highlanders, Welsh Regiment. Cheshire Regiment, Derby Regiment, and Middlesex Engineers. These Volunteer contingents numbered over 1,000. They were cheered by friends as they stepped on shore. Enthusiastic Scenes at Chester. . The Volunteer Service Comnany ef the Cheshire Reel- ment returned to Chester on Monday from south Africa and were the recipients of a most enthusisstic and patriotic welcome home. The cony .ny reached South- ampton on the previous ewning, and, according to the original arrangement, should have arrived at Chester shortly before two o'cloels in the afternoon, but owing to Several causes they did not arrive until six o'clock in the evening. The company proceeded to Satoh Africa 126 strong under the command of Captain Thornely, of the 2nd V.B. Cheshire Regiment, and Lieutenant Races, of Stalybridge. they have been under fire twice, at Brandford and Z tnd River, and they were participants in Lord Roberts's advance up country. Several of the men have been invalided flame, and the number who returned yesterday was 103 men and Itsve officers. The chief thoroughfares of the city were decorated with bunting, and presented a gay appearance. The men were met at the station by detachments of the let Cheshire and Carnarvonshire Volunteer Artillery, under the command of Major Mason, and of the 2nd V.B. Cheshire Regiment, ender Colonel Smith,with the bands of the Depot Cheshire Regiment and of the two ' Volunteer corps named. In the Te*n Hall Square there was a crowd of about ten thousand people. Toe healthy and bronzed appearance of the men was the subject of general comment. The men were afterwards entertained at dinner in the Town Ball. Runcorn's Reception of her Soldier Sons. Beautiful weather prevAiled on Tuesday, and the lags, bunting and other decorative devices displayed by the inhabitants of the town, in honour of the home- coming of "Runcorn's Soldiers of both Queen and King" dashed and glinted in the bright sunlight, from morning till eve, in delightful harmony with the spirits and sympathies of the townspeople." " News ! News of the War ! Another victory for Nelson !" in years agone was the cry that filled each city, town and hamlet with the acclaims of a cheerful joyful people, whose joy was ever tempered with thankfulness. The news of the return of the Special Service Com. pany, Paid B Atation Cheshire Regiment,from the seat of war, and the announcement that four of the Runcorn men,who went out:some 15 months ago, were returning to their homes by thee 30 pm train from Chester,rekindled the spirit of yore, aruf the scene in Runcorn streets on Tuesday evening bill, el description. The pitlel was dense with people animated with a cheerful jollity which had to be witeeised to be duly appreciated. In short the town rose to the occasion and honoured its "brave" right gallantly. It will be remembered that the men who went from Runcorn about 15 months ago, and who were gener- ously entertained by Mr S Taylor, J.P., Rydal Mount, included :—Lance Sergeant F J Jeacock (who ranked as sergeant), Lance Corporal F J Speakman ; Privates L , Mack, F Platt, D Chadwick and A C Timmins, The I first four were returning, Private Chadwick having I secured a Government appointment as fitter on the railway, sni Private Timmins, a post at the station in Pretoria, being left behind in South Africa. THE SCENE AT THE STATION. The F and G Companies, 2nd Earl Cheshire RegirnOnt Volunteer Battalion, under Captain George F Ashton (commander) and Captain Timmins, were drawn up on the platform ready to welcome their comrades. The hand, about 2 with buglers, were in attendance under 3 tor maattr Outhwaite, and there were also on parade Quarter-master Sergeant Hankinsen and Sergeant Wood- land (retired list) ; .Sergeant Instructor Callaghan, Colour Sergeant Harvey, Sergeants Platt, Rushton, Holmes, Edwards, Lea, Phoenic and Matthews; Lance- Sergeants Gittens and Gaikelt and but 100 rank and file. The railway officials were also present and contributed laying when fot hz -es g tnraalisn av; their share to theitrechepatoipoennebdy salute. Thus eliding up to the platform, the congested mass of humanity out, ide the station premises, were made aware of its proximity and raised a tremendous cheer. This had hardly died away when the Band struck up" Soldiere of the Queen," and the
r :

men who had gone out as such realised they returnedas "Soldiers of the Bing." Forming into quarter colanin, headed by the Baud, and with the four" Volunteer Soldiers" in the post of honour, the whole moved off by Station-road and Waterloo-road to the Town Hall.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY, MAY 3 1901.
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY, MAY 3 1901.
AT: THO TOWN HALL.

Mr W Handley (vice-chairman), in the alumna Of Mr R H Posnett (the chairman) with Messrs S Taylor J.F., E Imison, J.F., C.C., F .1 Norman, George Hewitt' .1 Wilsen.lT Dean, S Walton, E G.tley, T Jones, J H Salkeld, D Bisbrown, E Marshall, James Wilding and other gentlemen were waiting, and upon the arrival of the procession. Mr Handley shook hands with the four returned men, and extended to them a very hearty welcome on behalf of the town. Addressing them Mr Flandl.y said : I was his pleasure and privilege to welcome them home to their native town, families, and friends. (Applause.) Fifteen months ago they left home at the call of duty. Since then how short the time had been, and yet how full of varied experiences. Hardships, discomforts,su ffLeings had not been unknown to them Some of them MIR been brought low by sick- ness and yet they had borne all with patience. if not with perseverance, in the cause of their country. ehey had seen the horrors of war ae well ,t/R partaken of the glories of victory. (Cheers.) At Z ind River, Brand. fort, Karee, and Rustenburg the- thunder of battle had sounded in their ears, Cempatriets had fallen at their sides, and yet they had been spared to return to their anxious /- rents their country, and their homes. (Cheers.) They de- voutly joined with them in thankfulness to ild for His great mercies, and rejoiced with them in their reinic'eg. N-ither would they forget the two who remained in the far-off country. As their kith and kin they were links binding them in interest and sympathy. and they trust- ed that in their new home they might have peace and Prosperity. (Cheers.) When the Runcorn Volun- teers were first formed in Runcorn (of whom there were but few left) it was never anticipated that its members would ever be required for active service abroad. But sooner than the actual need arose 47 of their citizen army volunteered—(c !seers) —although but six were asked for. In their rejoicing that day they would not forget those who if yet needed would be ready ,to respond to the call of King and country. ((beers). At the time of its inception one of our townsmen, who had lona since passed from the sphere of this life printed and published some verses entitled the Rencorn Volunteers, two of which slightly adopted to change seemed to have been prophetic They hold in detestation The thought or shedding blood. But to defend the nation They'd fight by field and filood. And with their trusty rifles With hearts that know no fears. Her fame shalt be protected, By the Runcorn Volunteers. That England dreads no tyrant, For her sons with freedom blessed. Will keep her flag triumphant, Oer sea and ocesn'at;reast ; And, when she needs defending, As onward roll the years. She'll never want for heroes, In her Runcorn Volunteers' (Loud cheers).

The reembr,rs of the Claud! Wm shook hands with the " four khaki clad horoes;" and three hearty cheers having ben givn by tiv, asPPmbled populace, the pro- cession reormed and headed by the Council, with the deputy-chairman wearing thP chaiu of office, moved by way of Church-street,llih.strest and Greenway-road to the

div.head: DRILL HILL.
div.p: DRILL HILL.

Arrived her/the Band played "God save the King." Captain George F Ashton said he had the pleasure of saying a few words to them in that hall 15 months pre- viously when they were about to depart for South Africa. He then wished them well on behalf of the Runcorn Detachment. (Cheers.) He now wished to express the delight of the &tatchment at seeing them safely back again in that hall, (Cheers) Six of them had gone away, but only four of them were returned, but he was glad to see they had escaped that disease, which had been the fate of so many of their comrades in South Africa. After their own relatives, he did not think there was anyone who more heartily wished them safely back again in 'their native country than did the inemb,re of the F and G Companies who saw them off 15 months previously. (Cheers.) At Chester he hal spoken to CaptainTeorneley about them, and Captain Thorneley told him something which made him feel very proud of them. (Cheers.) He told him (Captain Ashton) that he could not speak,with regard to the men from Runcorn, in aey war too highly of them. (Cheers.) He thought that Was quite good ecough coming from their officer. The Detachment felt proud—as proud as it Was possible for them to be—of the men who went to s,uth Africa from their ranks. (Cheers.) Their names would live with the Detachment as Inng as the Runcorn Volunteer Corps existed, and he only hoped they might have such's future as they deserved. (Loud cheers.) The men were then dismissed. Two of the men Lance-Sergeant Jeacock and Lance- Corporal Speakman, who reside in flatten, were then escorted by the Band to their native village, and both received a reception well worthy of the occasion.
Runcorn Volunteers to be Rewarded.

Mr E Imison, C.C., J.P., at the meeting of the Runcorn Urban District Council, on Thursday morning, referred to the fact tbst thelphoto of the Ru r corn Volun- teers, who formed the Ru3corn portion of the Second Cheshire B ittalion, Special Service Corps,had been hung in the Connpil Chamber, and urged that tbe chairman should give the to wnspeopl. an opportunity of doing sornething in the way of showing their due appreciation of the men's self denial, by calling a public meeting, as there was a strong feeling abroad that something besides that already accomplished should be done. _ _ _

The vice-chairman (Mr Handley) said he would com- municate with Mr. Poanett the chairman, and willingly act in accord with his views on the subject. Mr Imison approached after the meeting gave it as his opinion,that some tangible gift—(such as a presenta- tion watch)—should be given the men, and that any function should he of a public character, and no t dependent upon any private effort. The matter was most cordially received by the whole Council. Frodsham, An Unique Spectacle.

In all its history, the village of Frodsham never ex- called itself more in beauty,tban on Tuesday evening last, when the residents put forth their best endettrours,in the decoration of Church and main streets,in honour of the return of six of the local membrs of the 2nd Cheshire Battalion, Special Service Corps.

• Trees which occupy a prominent aspect in both the streets named are just about putting on their foliage, and the delicate green of the tender spring shoots, formed a glorious sett log for the bunting and triumphant arches which reached from side to side of those magnificent thoroughf &res. Added to this some 12 to 15 thousand people were abroad, mostly in holiday attire, and the glint of the van-coloured hats and costames, especially of the female portion of the vast concourse, rendered the sight a truly magnificent one, The approaching of the train was heralded by a volley of fog signals, and the Band of the Frodshatn Volunteers struck up the " Conquering Hero," whilst from the throats of the assembled multi- tude went up a cheer, the spontaneousness and magni- tude of which testified their feelings in no mistakable degree. Drawn up on the platform were the Frodsham Companies: of the 2nd Earl Cheshire Volunteer Batta- lion, under Major Harrison, their band, and a large num- ber of the principal residents of the village. And as the men alighted Major Harrison accorded them a hearty welcome home. Subseqoently a move was made to the Drill Hall, where'the men were warmly received by their comrades. Their names are : Sergeant Holland, Corporal George Rogers, Lance• Corporal Carvier, Lance-Corporal Evans, Private Carter and Private Darlington. After being dismissed, the Band escorted Corporal Rogers to his home, and played several selections in his honour as prior to his going to South Africa he filled the important position of their conductor.

div.head: Return of Lymm Volunteers.
div.p: Return of Lymm Volunteers.

The Lynam contingent of the Cheshire Special Service Volunler Company had a grand reception on their arrival on Tuesday night from South Africa. Two bands were out, and a torchlight procession was spontaneous- ly organized, and the whole village turned out to give the men a hearty. welcome home. Arriving at the Drill Hall, Captain Graves stated that he was proud to wel- come Corporal Clare and Private Leigh. They looked right well.

The May isszie of the DarPsbury Parish Magazine contains the following :—"Tue patron of the living of Daresbury, Sir G Greenell, has offered it to the Rev Frederick Clifton Smith, senior curate of Tar- porley and he has accepted it Mr. Clifton Smith is a graduate of Cambridge University and has been curate of Torporley ever since he was ordained in 1894. H? will not be able to take up his residence at Dares. bury at present, but whenever he comes we trust he will get a hearty welcome from the parishioners. The Rev S W Dunn, curate-in-charge, has now left the parish,and preached his last sermon and said "farewell" on the evening of Sunday, April 2lst. He has taken a curacy at Guisborough in Yorkshire where we trust he will have better health than he hne unfortunately experienced in Moore. It is hoped that the services of the Rev H A Lester may be retained until the new vicar climes."

div.head: NOTES ON (JAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. [By " Ovalist.']
div.p: NOTES ON (JAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. [By " Ovalist.']

Not a single cup after all—except the cup of sorrow— and the cheeriest optimist couldn't gloat over that. Last time I penned this weekly column WM were all of us in Warrington living in hopes and fond expeco.iions of having toot° the Northern Union and West Lsncashire Cups to feist our eyes noon as the lawful fruits of con- quest. Vain hopes! The Warrington rivn failed lamentably on Saturday, and a co .:.bination of circum- ,t.nces as prevented tkae acquisition of oven the West Lancashire trophy. Let me explain.

There problbly never was more confidence in a foot- ball team than there was in toe Warrington lot, among their friends, on Saturday. They had performed so consistently rand even brilliantly throughout the Cup tourney that there seemed no reason in the world why they should not successfully surmount the last hurdle, Batley's fame as cup-fighters, notwithstanding. A com- parison of results was all in favour of the Lancashire team, whoss prolific scoring ham'. been the source of general eminent, and the defence was voted amply good enough. But these proved to b 3 the considerations that weighed least in the final struggle.

Without proceeding any further I May at once say that Warrington were fairly and squirely beaen, but they would not have been but for nad management in several directions and acute " stage-fright " among the players. The latter was the chief cause of the break- down and of the really poor show Warrington made before the 33,000 people who agsembled to witness the contest. Nervousness was, of course, expected in so young a team and one entirely strange to the excite- ments of a cup-final. But nobody anticipated that it would have had the paralysing effect on the nara that it undoubtedly had. Such '• funk' one can hardly for- give after the manly fashion In which other severe struggles have been got through, but it is repugnant to me to blame the lads themselves. Unfortunately the inimanagement mentioned had a good deal to do with the state of nervousness in which the players were , found at the critictl moment, and consequently the Isame thing is responsible in great measure for the loss of the Cup.

It seems to be elect that the Warrington team arrived at Headingley sometime before the match, and that the players were actually stripped for the fray an hour be.pre time. Not only this—which is silly enough—but they were confined in a small, stuffy room smelling of paint land with nothing to do except twiddle their thumbs and make each other nervous by thinking and talking of the ordeal shortly to be gae through. Could anything be more insane ? It is well-known that the best and coolest athletre feellsomething of " funk" before a big event if they are given time to ponder over it. Anything of the kind should have been avoided as much as possible on Saturday, and if the players had been brought to the ground at the last minute, or taken for a drive or walk beforehand, they would have turned out much fitter for the task before them than they did. Though it is "easy to be wise after the event," I should not have imagined that any memb qs of the Warrington Committee could have acted so foolishly, and those responsible are much to blame for the fiasco which occurred.

The hopes of Lancashire, as well as Warrington.rested on the" wire-pullers," and it is no secret that the chief officials of the Lancashire C mspetitiou were sadly dis• appointed at the poor show made by Warrington. They knew as well as anybody what sort of a game Warring- ton could play, and it was a bitter blow to them to see the Cup going back to Yorkshire after such a poor effort to keep it in the County Palatine.

Warrington played by far the worst game they have played for a long time. There was a lack even of dash, and nervousness is surely no excuse tor that. The for- wards might not have been trying they did so badly both in the scrimmage and in following-up. They were by no means the speedy, vigorous eight we have been accustomed to see. Their bad failure resulted in the halVes being overpowered and the tbreequarters practi- cally lapttled up, though the backs mignt have done much better as it was. Bate was slow when smartness was the one thing needful, and poor Fish never got a chance to show the metal he is made of. He played finely, nevertheless,and the same may be said of El illand who showed none of the hesitation which spoiled the game of his colleagues. He had the hardest luck in not securing a couple of tries by fins following-up, while his punting and defensive play were really grand.

As a spectacle the math did not rank high. Batley are not a very scientific team, and Warrington's clever- ness was comp.etely hidcien,sso that open, interesting movements were not of frequent occurrence. The first score came after ten minutes play,and was due to a bad pass by Isherwood to Dickenson. The latter could not field the ball, and Oakland nipped in smartly. He ran strongly for the line and at the right moment passed to Watty "Davies who got an easy try. Davies was "off "at goalkicking all afternoon and made no sort of a kick from his own try. Try the second—and last— was got by quick passing among the Batley backs, who were lined out near the Warrington line. Auty was the scorer and he had little more to do than drop over at the corner. Batley's position near the line was due to a , bad kick by Dickenson i and thus both the tries were in some measure the result of faulty play by the Warring- ton backs rather than the cleverness of the Yorkshire attack. This was all the scoring and Warrington letting several chances go by were beaten pointless by two tries (6 points).

Isherwood adopted a very questiognaabaleestwicemotuorrsdneotfwahlioleeendt he chOse to play against the wind after winning the toss, aafgarinsrt cmeeurning, Fish had w and the poaligcayinwsthßicah aid Batley. Still the tma:soheariy penaltyf-btlime .kickslmmediately a dt goal iately after from good positions—one being right opposite even—but like Davies, his goal- kicking powers were sadly wanting, and the ball went wrong each time. Bad either of these goals been kicked I think Warrington might have won. They just wanted 1 some such encouragement, and it was the hardest luck that a try which Harris or Duckworth got in the first five minutes of the match wi,s not allowed. A goal or a try would have done much to counteract the nervous- ness, which seemed to go worse as Batley drew ahead. What luck there was knocking about did not come War- rington's way, it is certain. I must give Batley credit for winning the Cup for the third time in five years. Their performance is a fine one, and in many respects they are a fine team They possess a defence which is every bit as good as it is said to b, and a finer set of tacklers I never saw. Forwards and backs alike seemed to p 055385 the faculty of being in two places at once, and whenever a Warrington man xot away he was generally bowled over by at least a couple of opponents. The forwards are a grand lot, and that 15 the art of scrummaging that they do t there is worth knowing Also, they are Enhoe heavier than Warrington. though the published weights point to an opposite conclusion. The back play of the Batley team was not very brilliant but it had the merit of effectiveneas. There was generally some quick pass- ing and short dashes when near the line, but they had little knowledge of travelling down the field with passing runs after the manner of the Lancashire teams. Their absolute reliability and fine kicking powers were the strongest points of the Batley backs, though Davies is a player of superior class. He seems to be just such another as Fish for speed and resource. Garner (full back), was the weak man of the team, and if Warrington had been smarter they might have profited by his mis- takes.

Turning—and with some relief—from the match it- self, I must withdraw all previous compliments paid to the railway companies. Their arrangements on Satur- day broke down in a fashion nothing short of shameful. Of the Pre or six thousand enthusiastic Warringtonians who left fn' L'OCI9 in the special trains, not one third were on ti • • ground when the play commenced, and the ' welcoming cheer Warrington got therefore was not very encouraging, especially compared with the huge roar of applause which greeted Batley. The numerous Yorkshire specials into Leeds made matters most awkward, but all such difficulties could have been and should have been foreseen. The trains from War- rington could easily have started an heur earlier, and then, perhaps, thousands of workingmen who bad saved for this especial occasion would not have been defrauded of their hard-earned pleasure. Hundreds came in after half time, while many never got to Headingley at all. The whole thing is a disgrace to the companies con- cerned, and it is a pity their directors were not within hearing distance of some of the aggrieved ones. As it was an engine-driver blushed. There was one incident rcmte which has its funny side. During. one of the many stoppages, a number of excursionists jumped out on the line and about half 'of 'em got left, while the re- mainder risked their Lives in scrambling back into the departing train. What the lone lost ones said or did in the middle of the Yorkshire moors, I know not, but their case was one calling for some ingenuity in the employ- ment of the" mother-tongue,"

Both players and spectators took their defeat very well, and not a few were glad it was all over, the excite- ment having been rather trying. As runners-up the Warrington men received handsome gold methls, and w, re, therefore, not entirely unrewarded for their ora— tions.

It is pretty well understood that the Northern Union takes the whole of the gate-money in the final tie. The competing club. however, are granted £5O each, and this seasen an effort is being made to get a proper share of the proceeds. There is no need for the Union to heard , up gold, and Warrington may yet handle some of the £1,650 taken at lieadingley. By the way, what a fine sight flan huge concourse of 33.000 spectators presented in the brilliant atternoon sun !

Warrington and Leigh made a pointless draw of the final t)e fir the South-Wes Lancashire and B mler Towns Cup on Monday evening at Wigan, after the most fiercely contested gams I ever remember Seeing. 111-luck seems to be dogging Warrington's steps now, and they would probably have secured the West Lancashire Cup, but for the fact that they were cirripelled to take the field short of five of the mm who took part in Saturday's match. The substitutes did yeoman service and the result of the encounter is certainly a credit to Warring- ton seeing that Leigh had their best team on and all the men were in perfect condition. Even then they could not beat Warrington as they have long been threatening to do, and the honours of the game were very evenly divided.

Leigh had come with the clear intention of laying out "some of the Warrington men, and in the first two minutes Ratcliffe fell a victim to an exccedm-dv foul charge by Ganley. Fish was also mauled by Davies, and Burgess and Me-eweather likewise got roughly handlod. Fortunately for Warrington they all recovered and kept their plac.s. Mr Kidd was not firm enough, and by simply cautioning three or four Leigh men he merely encouraged their brutality. This sort of thing notwithstanding, the match was a magnificent one to watch, for excitement was at full pressure during the whole of the 70 minutes and the pace of the play was truly remarkable. The Vi,arrington forwards plavel like veritable fiends, and half the " devil " they put into their play would have sufficed to turn the scale in Saturday's encounter. There was no nervousness on Monday,and the whole team played excellently. Burgess and Allen got through a lot of work at half and though not very clever at the passing game, I think they would have made more progrees than Duckworth and Bate on Saturday. Hallam and the whole of the threequarters were tip-top considering what they had gone through.

On the Leigh aide Danbavi—n 'Wag the shining light, hi. play all through being superb. Tnere is no doubt that Leigh would have been badlv beaten but for his relia- bility at critical moments, and never-ending resource. The front rank out-lasted Warrington towards the close, but the backs never looked much like piercing the War- rington defence. Even drop-kicking was off, neither Dunbavin nor Molvrea' being able to pilot the ball between the sticks. Warrington had some narrow escapes in this line, and the tension was great near the close when Molvneux had two place-kicks opposite Vl- pee's. Greater still was the relief when the ball hit the Warrington forwards for the second time.

Tnern was a big crowd, hut the proceeds ought to have been £lOO instead of MT. The Wigan club's bad management resulted in the stand being rusted by the Warrington crowd and filled up free, while later on the gates were burst and a second lot obtained a gratis view of the game. Wigan's "fixtures" do not make a very valuable asset, and the club must be near the bank- raptcy court judge by the state of stand, fences, etc. Most of the wood-work broke uale]s you trod very cargully.

, It W-IS too dark to play extra time, so the Leigh officials clamoured for a match the following evening. Warrington refused—both players and officials—arid offered to play at Widnes on Saturday with free admis- sion. This L,igh declined, and as Warrington were firm Igif,l3 went to Widnes on Tuesdayland amuged them selvei by claiming the cup in forfeit. They have not got it, however. It was too much to expect the Warrington men to turn out on Tuesday, seeing that not one was free from injury. As a matter of fact only two of the players have worked since Friday, and six of thorn are even now" on the club." Probably the West Lancashire Coo will not be played for again, and Warrington and Leigh will have to 133 considered joint owners.

The Warrington Works Competition ended on Tues- day, when Crosfield's defeated Richmond's in the final tie after a rially excellent game. Councillor Pierpoint presented the medals, and made an interesting speech on sport and pastime ia general. It is satisfactory to learn that the receipts exceed those of last season, and a good sum will again b 3 devoted to charities.

div.head: Cricket.
div.p: Cricket.

The suggested alteration of the cricket law of " leg before wicket " was discuzised at the annual meeting sif the Matylebono Club on Wednesday. Thr matter was put to the vote, and the proposal was supported by 259 members and opposed by 188 The majority in its tavour was thus 71, but as this did not reach the two- thirds majority necessary for an alteration the law re- mains unchanged. The law in its present flrm reads : " The striker is out if with any part of his person he ston the ball, which in the opinion of the umpire at the bowler's wicket shall have been pitched in a straight line from it to the striker's wicket, and would have hit It—' leg before wicket.'" For this it sa as proposed to substitute " The striker is out if with any part of his person (except the hand) which is between wicket and wicket he intercept a ball which would bit his wicket— leg before wicket.'"

The Warrington team should have met Rush°hue on Saturday but owing to the football cup final at Leedq, the eneazement was cancelled. Te-day's fixture is with Cheadle Hulrne and the match takes place on the ArpleV *admire.

Sankey Wire Mills contingent journeyed to Golborne on Saturday. The home team bartPd first and compiled 115 runs, Entwistle knockinir up 28 in fine style. The visitor? score had reached 28 runs for tbe logs of three wickets *ben rain commenced to fall and the match was abandoned.

The Warrington Police team played their opening engagement of the season on Tuesday, when they met the Co-operative Stores emplot 63. The local represen- tatives of law and order fared badly on this occasion, retiring defeated by a majority of 33. For the winners, Johnson wrought great havoc with the ball, taking seven wickets for eight runs. That player also gave the most creditable exhibition of batting, his contribution being 14 runs. None of the policemen reached double figures.

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.

POLICE CASES, At the Earlestown Police 6tation on Monday morning before 1r J W Emmett, James Etigeley Baker, of Wargrave-road, Farlestawn, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Harlestown on Saturday night, an 1 was duel 54 and costs. John Murphy of Clarence-street, E alestown was tined 2:s 61 and costs for a similar offence the same night. _

Sr. JOHN'S CHURCH, -EARLESTOWN. The annud special services in aid of the schools connected with the above place of worship were held in the Courch on Sunday. The morning and afternoon preacher was the Rev H I Wadeson rector of Croft, and in the evenintz the pulpit was occupied by the Rev F A Screeton. At each of the services there were large congregations, and special hymns were sung by the choir and children. The collections throughout the day amounted to a little over £l3, an increase of about £3 over last year.

THE WARGRAVE SALE OF WORK. Salo of Work was opened ou Friday after- noon by the Rev J Car-on, recior of Wargrave. There was only a small attendance, but this was considerably augmen'ed in the evening,and towarde 10 o'clock the stalls wore a deserted and empty appearance. The sale was bro ight to acl )se by a social gathering at which there was a good number present. Dancing was started at 8 o'clock, and kept up with spirit until midnight, a most enjoy- able evening being spent. A very pleasing break in the programme, was the skirt dancing of four of the scholars of Wargrave school who had been excellently tutored by Mrs Chandlov, theiedancing being very much admired. They o•cupied the middle of the floor of the school- room, and the various steps were executed without a fault. The cl-ver little dancers were Misses L Silk, Nellie Josephs, Ada Oubridge, and Evelyn Holt, whilst Miss May Porter played the piano for the dancing. All the children were dressed in an 'appropriate costume which had a becoming effect. The proceeds from the sale and social amounted to abut £100.•

Ties anniversary services in aid of the funds of the school connected with the above body were held in the chapel on Funday. The morning-and evening services were conducted by the Rev E Dies el Maimle, who was formerly s..ationsid at Eirle,town. Mr Davies was highly esteemed when he was resident at Earlestown, and recently there was a large gathering of friends at ths services SptTial hymns were sung by the choir and children and at each service an on.hem was rendered by the choir.ln the morning the anthem was" Behold G id is my Salvation,"the solo being given by Mr G Edmonds jun., and in the evening Worthy to be praised," solo by Mis+ Woods, and quartette by Misses Woorls and M Banton, Messrs A Banten and E Mullins. In the aftsrnoon the choir rendered in very good style the cantata " The City of G 31,1? Excellent time was kept. tied the parts were' well balanced. Mr W Aa conducted and the accompanists were Miss Tocieobs and Mr Andy L.mond. The principal seloiste were Mies .8 Woods, A Dickens, F Tombs, G lmonds. Stronach, Baxter, Messrs J Sproston, Hatton,Mullinsj Banton G Edmond+ and A Banton The collections during the day am einted to over £4B a consilerable increase on last year. THEFT AT NEWTON.—THE RESULT OF INTRWPERANCE. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday before Mr John White and other magistrates, a respectably dressed man named William Smith, who stated that, he was a lo ksmrti by trade, was charged with stealing an albert and medal and two vests value £3 10i, the property of William Smith. 37, Mill-lane, Newton, some time between 10 p.m. on April 23rd an" 730 a.m. on April 24th.—He pleaded guilty. -William smith, a collier, residing at 37. Mill-lane, Newton, stated that on Wednesday evening April 24'h he returned from work. On going into his bedroom he found the articles mentioned in the charge were missing The prisoner had slept in the same bedroom on Monday and Tuesday nights.lnformation was given fro the police and later ou, witness identified the articles produced at the Earlestown Police Station as his property—Nellie Pritchard, wife of Richer 1 Pritchard, a pawnbroker, carrying on business at, 31, Msrket-street, Earlestown, said that at 8.30 on Wednesday morning, the 24th ult, prisoner came into the shop and offered to pledge two vests. Witness asked him if they belonged to him and prisoner replied that they did. He said he was out of work and wanted money to go to Warrington to start at a new place.. She advanced him 3+ 64 on the vests.—Henry Morris, pawnbroker, 42. Market- street stated that the prisoner pledged the albert , and medals at his shop for 3s 6d. He said they had , been given to him as a debt.—P.C. Hughes said he apprehended the prisoner and charged him with the offence and he made no reply.—Prisoner in- formed the magistrates that the theft was the result of the folly of drinking. He wanted to get drink and seeing the articles in the bedroom he took than on the impulse of tbe moment and pledgedlhem.—lt was stated that prisoner had not been before the Court previously. He had been in custody since Saturday.—The magistrates took a lenient view of the case and sentenced him to one day's imprisenment,—Prisoner promised never to tekr-So drink again and thanked the Bench for their Vnijincy.

, _ GOOD • TBNIPLARY. The Hope of Earlestown Lodge held a reunion of the past and present members of this Lodge in the Co-operative Hali, Wargrave-road, Bro Williamson Presiding. The meeting was opened by singing " Elark, the temperance bells are ringing." Bro Williamson, in his opening remarks, welcomed all present,and said he had been surprised and startled by reading of the growth and extent of the Order, which 50 years since was just beginning to grow, and was confined to North America, being after- wards extended to the British Isles, trom which it has spread to all parts of the world,and is now work ing in 100 countries, states and territories, and has about 13,000 Lodges and temples meet- ing weekly, wish about 550,000 members. At the close of his address the following pro- gramme was rendered : Reading, entitled " ex tail soup, Bro Warburton; song, "Twopenny toll," Sim Williams ; recitation, " Curfew shall not ring to-night," Sis Ord ; song, "The blue alsatian mountains." Sis Morley. Bro Lindon, V.D. on rising to address the meeting said he was glad to be present. He had been a member of the Order for 30 years, and still had a vivid recollection of the early days of the Order and of the work done. People had an idea that the members of the Order confined their work to their own Lodges, but they worked hard in other societies and had started some of them, such as the British Womens Society, which was first started in the Grand Lodge. rhey had also worked hard in defeating the compensation clauses. Bro Dring proposed a vote of thanks to Bro Lindon, which was secdnded by Bro Macklin, and was heartily accorded. Refresh- ments were then handed round by Sisters Mrs Williams, Mrs Chapman, Mrs Owens, Miss boslin and Miss Wright. The ode "Sound the battle cry,"wns then sung by the members. Bro Wood, L.D. invited all old members to rejoin and fight against the only enemy England has to fear. An enemy whose ravdges they felt just as much in Earlestown as in Liverpooi. He had joined the Order not because he had personally any need, but he felt it his duty to do all he could to stem the tide of intemperance. The Order Was s religious one, hut was not denominational,ol sections of the Christian church being represented in it. Song, "The Heavenly city," Sister Goslin, was well ren- dered, but the lateness of the hour prevented an encore, the meeting being closed with prayer by Bra Driag.

Among the wounded is General Zerpitzki.
